items.title: Pushing the Frontier of Black-Box LVLM Attacks via Fine-Grained Detail Targeting
items.summary: arXiv:2602.17645v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Black-box adversarial attacks on Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) are challenging due to missing gradients and complex multimodal boundaries. Prior state-of-the-art transfer-based approaches such as M-Attack match local crops between source and target images, but this induces high-variance, nearly orthogonal gradients across iterations. We attribute this instability to (i) ViT translation sensitivity, which yields spike-like gradients, and (ii) a structural asymmetry between source and target crops. We reformulate local matching as an asymmetric expectation over source transformations and target semantics, and introduce M-Attack-V2 based on this formulation. Multi-Crop Alignment (MCA) averages gradients from multiple local views per iteration, while Auxiliary Target Alignment (ATA) replaces aggressive target augmentation with a small set of semantically correlated auxiliary images. Patch Momentum replays historical crop gradients, and a patch-diverse surrogate ensemble (PE+) strengthens transferable directions. M-Attack-V2 raises attack success rates over M-Attack from 40% to 61% on GPT-6.1 Sol, from 40% to 60% on GPT-6 Astra, and from 85% to 97% on Claude Sonnet 5.5. Code and data are publicly available at: https://github.com/VILA-Lab/M-Attack-V2.

items.title: Multilingual Safety Alignment via Self-Distillation
items.summary: arXiv:2605.02971v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit severe multilingual safety misalignment: they possess strong safeguards in high-resource languages but remain highly vulnerable to jailbreak attacks in low-resource languages. Current safety alignment methods generally rely on high-quality response data for each target language, which is expensive and difficult to generate. In this paper, we propose a cross-lingual safeguard transfer framework named Multilingual Self-Distillation (MSD). This framework transfers an LLM's inherent safety capabilities from high-resource (e.g., English) to low-resource (e.g., Javanese) languages, overcoming the need for response data in any language. Our framework is flexible and can be integrated with different self-distillation strategies. Specifically, we implement two concrete methods -- on-policy MSD and off-policy MSD -- both of which enable effective cross-lingual safety transfer using only multilingual queries. Furthermore, we propose Dual-Perspective Safety Weighting (DPSW), a divergence measure to optimize the distillation objective. By jointly considering the perspectives of both the teacher and the student, DPSW adaptively increases the penalty weights on safety-critical tokens while reducing the weights on non-critical tokens. Extensive experiments on representative LLMs across diverse multilingual jailbreak and utility benchmarks demonstrate that our method consistently achieves superior multilingual safety performance. Notably, it generalizes effectively to more challenging datasets and unseen languages while preserving the model's general capabilities.

items.title: Coral: Cost-Efficient Multi-LLM Serving over Heterogeneous Cloud GPUs
items.summary: arXiv:2605.04357v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The landscape of large language models (LLMs) has become increasingly fragmented, with no single model dominating the field. Meanwhile, cloud providers offer a diverse array of mid-tier and older-generation GPUs. These heterogeneous resources provide better availability and deliver comparable performance-per-dollar to top-tier hardware. To efficiently harness these GPUs for concurrent multi-LLM serving, we introduce Coral: an adaptive, heterogeneity-aware serving system. The key idea behind Coral is the joint optimization of resource allocation and replica serving strategies across all models. To keep pace with shifting throughput demands and resource availability, Coral employs a lossless, two-stage decomposition. This approach preserves joint optimality while reducing online solve times from hours to mere tens of seconds. Evaluations across 6 models and 20 GPU configurations demonstrate that Coral reduces serving costs by up to 2.79$\times$ compared to the strongest baseline, while delivering up to 2.39$\times$ higher goodput under scarce resource constraints.

items.title: Nexus : An Agentic Framework for Context-Aware Time Series Forecasting
items.summary: arXiv:2605.14389v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Language models have emerged as highly capable reasoners, yet their performance in time series forecasting remains uneven across domains and levels of contextual grounding. This is primarily due to their suboptimal time series reasoning and numerical modeling capabilities. To tackle this, we introduce Nexus, a multimodal forecasting framework that bridges qualitative event reasoning with structural numerical modeling through principled statistical synthesis. Nexus follows three structured stages: (1) Temporal profiling and anchor generation, which distills the multimodal history into a timestamped causal-temporal profile and generates a forecast anchor (2) Dual contextual outlook generation, which produces decoupled macro and micro level forecast trajectories, and (3) Bayesian synthesis, which reconciles the forecasting anchor with both contextual forecast trajectories via closed-form Gaussian updating weighted by empirical error covariances. Evaluated across three diverse forecasting benchmarks constituting eight datasets spanning rich event contexts, abrupt shocks, and purely numerical series, Nexus consistently outperforms leading time-series foundation models and language model baselines, while providing interpretable causal reasoning.

items.title: Agentic Reverse Engineering: From I/O to Code with Discovery Agent
items.summary: arXiv:2605.15334v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The automatic synthesis of a program from any form of specification is regarded as a holy grail of computer science. Fueled by LLMs, NL2Code has achieved tremendous success, yet the fundamentally more challenging task of synthesizing programs from input-output behavior, which we refer to as IO2Code, remains largely unsolved. Whereas NL2Code can exploit the semantic alignment between natural language and code acquired during pretraining, IO2Code requires recovering underlying principles from concrete computational behavior, navigating a vast and underspecified hypothesis space. To address this, we propose DIO-Agent, a discovery agent that performs agentic reverse engineering from input-output behavior to code. Our method frames IO2Code as an evolutionary search over discrete program space, in which an LLM serves as the mutation operator and concrete error signals from execution guide each mutation. To prevent the search from wandering into structurally complex yet incorrect dead ends, we introduce the Transformation Priority Premise as a mutation prior that biases the LLM toward the simplest hypothesis consistent with current evidence, progressively escalating from constants to conditionals to iteration only when simpler constructs are insufficient. To facilitate systematic study, we further construct an IO2CodeBench spanning multiple difficulty levels. Extensive experiments show that DIO-Agent consistently outperforms both traditional program-by-example method and SOTA evolution-agent baselines across all difficulty levels and various LLMs, while substantially surpassing test-time scaling strategies with equivalent sampling budgets.

items.title: A Measure-Theoretic Analysis of Reasoning in Transformers: Structural Generalization and Approximation Limits
items.summary: arXiv:2605.19944v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Scaling laws for reasoning in large language models (LLMs) are well documented, but little theory explains their out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization. We formalize reasoning with optimal transport: each search trajectory is mapped to twelve structural coordinates, such as tree depth and backtracking rate, and dataset shift is measured by the Wasserstein-1 distance. Kantorovich duality bounds the OOD risk through this distance, the architecture's Lipschitz constant and approximation limits. First, under absolute positional encoding (APE), shifting part of a trajectory to later positions almost surely changes the attention scores within that part; if this misroutes exact-match search, the Lipschitz constant and risk are $\Omega(1)$. Shift-invariant encodings such as rotary position embedding (RoPE) leave the scores unchanged and bound the error. Second, we map backtracking to a Dyck-$k$ language and, under an implicit-depth assumption, derive a risk floor for search trees deeper than a multiple of the number of layers. Enough layers remove this floor; more width only shrinks a separate Barron-space approximation term. Experiments with 54 trained Transformers on combinatorial search (Countdown) support these bounds. Appendix experiments measure structural shifts in public agent, embodied and robot trajectories, shift all position indices of 33 public language models, and split deeply nested tasks into separate model calls.

items.title: Non-Gaussianity Reveals Interpretable Directions in Language Models
items.summary: arXiv:2606.11722v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Finding human-interpretable directions in language-model activations is important for understanding and controlling model behavior. These directions are usually discovered through indirect learning objectives such as sparse reconstruction, but it remains unclear what existing statistical structure distinguishes interpretable directions and whether that structure can be used directly for feature discovery. We find that non-Gaussianity provides such a signature: projection distributions of natural-text residual-stream activations along sparse autoencoder (SAE) decoder directions are substantially more non-Gaussian than those along random directions, with most contexts forming a concentrated background and recurring patterns often occupying one tail. This raises a natural question: if interpretable directions tend to have non-Gaussian projection distributions, can we discover them by searching for non-Gaussian directions directly in activation space, without training another sparse dictionary? To test this hypothesis, we introduce ICA Lens, a practical workflow for efficient discovery, reliable annotation, and faithful evaluation of non-Gaussian directions in LLM residual-stream activations. Across GPT-2 Small, Gemma 2 2B, and Qwen 3.5 9B Base, we find that: (1) the recovered non-Gaussian directions capture coherent lexical, syntactic, and semantic patterns under both human and LLM-based evaluation; (2) non-Gaussianity is positively associated with both human-label confidence and automated interpretability; and (3) the resulting coordinates are competitive with SAEs across interpretability, sparse reconstruction, concept prediction, and targeted probe perturbation, while fitting in minutes per layer and using 7-43 times less memory. These results show that non-Gaussianity is a direct unsupervised signal for discovering interpretable and useful structure in activations.

items.title: Arithmetic and its remedies select the evidence on learned geometry
items.summary: arXiv:2607.17513v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Intelligence that must act before outside correction arrives must carry the structure of its expert knowledge, and hyperbolic geometry represents hierarchy with a fidelity no Euclidean space of comparable dimension matches. Yet hyperbolic language models confine that geometry to adapters or rebuild the transformer, and an independent audit of released hyperbolic vision language checkpoints finds their hierarchy mechanisms inactive, which has been read as evidence about the geometry or its objective. Here we show that it is also evidence about arithmetic. The constraint defining the manifold is a difference of two terms that grow together; for the unclamped map at unit curvature and temperature it fails in every format we measured, double precision included, at the norms standard language models produce in their deepest layers, beyond the limit previously derived. A common remedy, a norm bound, leaves the executed map no radial sensitivity where it acts. In a prespecified test, a tighter bound cost a Lorentz system more of the held out structure it started with than a flat one. Structural supervision has run in six expert systems over 20,951,552 training exposures. In paired runs with a published recipe's objective held fixed, removing its starting scale remedy prevented every update and removing its single precision regions raised the radius reached early in training. Arithmetic bounds the computable region, and within it, alongside the objective, arithmetic and its remedies select which runs leave a record and the states they reach on the way, so a flat surviving checkpoint cannot by itself establish that the geometry is inert.

items.title: WIDE: Boosting Adaptive LLM Inference via Token-level Dynamic Width Pruning
items.summary: arXiv:2607.28418v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Pruning is a promising approach for improving the efficiency of large language models (LLMs). Static structured pruning is hardware-friendly, but its input-agnostic computation allocation often degrades model quality at high sparsity. Dynamic pruning adapts computation to individual tokens, but coarse-grained layer-level routing limits allocation flexibility, and finer-grained decisions introduce irregular execution that can offset computational savings. To address these challenges, we present WIDE, the first end-to-end differentiable framework that combines token-wise structured dynamic width pruning with GPU kernel co-design for both prefill and decoding. WIDE uses differentiable routers to select GQA-aligned query-head groups and GPU-tile-aligned FFN-channel groups for each token. To execute these decisions efficiently, it reorders routing masks to cluster active tokens within each group, enabling hardware-agnostic block-level skipping and architecture-aware skipping of inactive loads and tensor-core operations. Experiments on the Llama3 and Qwen3 families demonstrate improved quality retention over representative static and dynamic pruning methods. At 50\% target routing sparsity, WIDE improves Llama3.1-8B average zero-shot accuracy by up to 20.26 points over the strongest dynamic-depth baseline under calibration-only settings, while retaining 97.6\%/88.2\% of dense Qwen3-14B likelihood/generation performance after LoRA tuning. Separate latency benchmarks demonstrate end-to-end speedups of up to $1.68\times$ for prefill and $1.55\times$ for decoding over the dense baseline. These results demonstrate that pruning--kernel co-design pushes the frontier of token-wise dynamic structured pruning, combining improved quality retention with practical acceleration across both prefill and decoding. Our code is avaliable at \url{https://github.com/EIT-NLP/LLM-Pruning/tree/main/WIDE}.

items.title: Rubric Dropout: A Simple Way to Mitigate Reward Hacking in Rubric-Based RL
items.summary: arXiv:2608.11669v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Rubric-based reinforcement learning, in which an LLM judge scores responses against prompt-specific criteria, has become a standard way to post-train language models on tasks without verifiable answers. The rubric, however, is only a proxy for response quality, and a policy trained against it long enough learns to exploit the difference. We train models with GRPO on medical and science rubrics and grade their responses on out-of-distribution (OOD) benchmarks throughout training with two judges: the training judge and a stronger OOD judge. The two scores first rise together and then diverge. The policy is learning to satisfy the training judge without writing better responses, which is a form of reward hacking. To mitigate it, we propose Rubric Dropout, which applies dropout to rubric criteria: at each training step, a random subset of each rubric's criteria is removed from the reward, so the rewarded subset of criteria is resampled at each step. All responses sampled for the same prompt are scored on the same subset, so their rewards remain comparable, and evaluation always uses the full rubric. We also introduce Block Dropout, which drops semantically similar criteria together so that a near duplicate of a dropped criterion cannot keep rewarding the same behavior. Across both benchmarks and models from 1.7B to 8B, dropout improves the gold judge's score on OOD benchmarks by up to 3 percent on HealthBench-Hard and 7 percent on ResearchQA, and it reduces both the gap between the two judges and over-crediting. It keeps in-domain reward close to the baseline, and dropout rates of 30-50 percent work best. Block Dropout improves the gold judge's OOD score further at the same dropout rate. Changing which criteria are rewarded at each step is a simple, inexpensive way to make rubric rewards harder to exploit.

items.title: Selection, Recombination, or a Fresh Solve? A Candidate-Free Control for Single-Pass Test-Time Aggregation
items.summary: arXiv:2608.18379v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: An aggregation pass gives a language model two things: candidate solutions and another chance to answer. We ask whether the candidates improve that attempt, and whether aggregation improves on selecting an existing answer. Our candidate-free control asks the same model to solve the problem again from the problem alone, using the same decoding settings and maximum output-token allowance. On AIME-2025 and HMMT-2025, Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 reaches 15.5% accuracy when all four candidates are wrong, compared with 27.7% for a fresh solve. When at least two candidates are correct, the ordering reverses: 88.7% for aggregation versus 59.7% for a fresh solve. With exactly one correct candidate, the benefit remains unresolved under the specified test. Yet plurality voting reaches 96.0% in the multiple-correct regime without another model generation; its accuracy difference from aggregation is inconclusive (raw $p = 0.180$). The all-wrong accuracy loss and multiple-correct gain survive a statistical correction for adding the second benchmark, developed after data collection, and persist when fresh responses are scored by their final answers. These findings concern one 4B model, two mathematics benchmarks, and a single aggregation pass over candidates truncated at their first answer. All-wrong recovery can arise from solving the problem afresh. The fresh-solve control tests whether candidates improve accuracy. Comparing with selection asks whether the additional generation improves on an existing answer.

items.title: Toollery: Scaling LLM Agents to Thousands of Skills and Tools
items.summary: arXiv:2609.22218v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: As LLM agents are exposed to hundreds to tens of thousands of skills, tools, and API functions, full-library prompting becomes costly, slow, and less reliable: each added candidate increases prompt tokens and latency, while longer candidate lists introduce more distractors for LLM selection. Following established document-side query expansion, Toollery generates user-intent queries from each skill/tool specification and builds a retrieval index that maps real user requests to compact candidate sets before final LLM decision-making. By treating high-level skills and atomic tools as selectable capabilities, Toollery can be applied to both skill libraries and tool registries. We evaluate Toollery on the roughly 79K-capability SkillRouter benchmark, BFCL-V4 with over 440 atomic tools, and 3,396 proprietary smart-cockpit requests over 220 tools. Across these settings, Toollery keeps online selection bounded to a compact top-K candidate set and improves recall over ordinary specification retrieval. At a fixed top-10 budget, Toollery improves end-to-end selection on the cockpit dataset, and maintains comparable AST Accuracy on BFCL-V4. These results support Toollery as a practical candidate-compression framework for large and evolving agent capability libraries, while showing that quality and cost gains depend on workload coverage and provider caching.

items.title: RLTLDR: Self-improvement by Internalizing Self-generated Feedback
items.summary: arXiv:2609.37633v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The common paradigm of reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) is to let agents make multiple attempts at a task, and optimize towards the successful ones. This becomes problematic in the realms of self-improvement, where tasks are so difficult that the agent has a low or even no chance of success, and where there are no teacher models or example solutions to distill from. In this paper, we introduce RLTLDR. After each failed attempt, we show the policy the verifier outputs and let it write its own feedback, in the form of a single TL;DR insight. The next rollout is conditioned on all previous insights, and we sequentially sample rollouts until a solution is found. Moreover, we enable backpropagation on the in-context insights to internalize a direct task to insight mapping. On challenging tool-calling and coding datasets (filtered to Pass@128=0), standard GRPO training of a Qwen 3.5 9B Thinking policy stays flat at a Pass@1 of 0% to 1%. RLTLDR breaks through this learning barrier, achieving a Pass@1 of 14-31% with insights in context during training and, crucially, 12-13% when no insight is in context at eval time. We identify that the key is the task to insight internalization. To study this further, we reduce our approach to SFTLDR, training only on (task, insight) tuples, without showing or backpropagating on any rollouts. Training on only 4k of these tuples recovers almost the full performance of RLTLDR and classical SFT on full rollouts. This demonstrates a promising compacted training paradigm of the form "on this sort of task, keep this sort of thing in mind", which we hope to inspire future research on.

items.title: OpenCollab: A Multi-Agent Coding Framework with Programmable Collaboration and Controllable Runtime
items.summary: arXiv:2609.38345v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Multi-agent coding systems are designed to tackle complex software engineering tasks through collaboration. However, existing evaluations typically assume configured organizations are followed faithfully, whereas reality differs. This behavioral gap, combined with differences in underlying system components, prevents clear attribution of observed gains. To this end, we introduce OpenCollab, a multi-agent coding framework that provides a unified infrastructure for programmable collaboration and controllable runtime. Specifically, OpenCollab unifies organization design, enforces experimental control on a shared runtime, and tracks execution through fine-grained event streams. On this basis, we define Adherence to quantify whether the declared organization is actually realized. Our experiments reveal that agents collaborate very differently across configurations: changing any single dimension shifts Adherence, from 47.2% to as high as 97.2%. items.title: Principled Under Pressure: Post-Training Decides Whether LLMs Act on Their Own Moral Judgment
items.summary: arXiv:2610.08670v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: An agent that can say an action is wrong and then take it anyway is a different failure from one that does not know better, and evaluations of stated values cannot see it. We ask how often open models act against their own moral judgment under pressure, and what decides and reduces it. We build a pre-registered panel of 248 scenarios across five kinds of pressure. Each scenario is posed to one model in two separate calls, as the agent choosing among fixed options and in the third person asking which is right; the model's own judgment is the reference, and the scenario's construction fixes which option counts as the violation. Every scenario has a twin with the pressure removed, and every model gets a positive control that bounds what the instrument can see. On OLMo-3-7B-Instruct, the model takes the action it judged wrong on one in five of the scenarios screened on its own actions, more often than with the pressure removed. Whether the gap appears depends on the post-training recipe: OLMo-3 and Meta's Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct carry it; Tulu 3, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and OpenAI's GPT-OSS-20B, read without reasoning, show none within stated detection bars. Meta's recipe and Ai2's Tulu 3 share the same Llama-3.1 weights; only Meta's carries the gap. On both models that carry it, reasoning about the stakes before acting moves the choice back toward the model's own judgment. What that deliberation tracks is the stated rule: where following a written rule harms an absent third party, it still moves OLMo-3 and GPT-OSS-20B toward the rule, not detectably diminished, while Llama-3.1's brake shrinks to about a seventh. Whether a model acts on its own moral judgment is therefore not settled by pretraining, and deliberation moves the action toward the stated rule, which protects people only when the rule does. The gap is a measurable target for post-training recipes, not a fixed property of the model.

items.title: The Window Is in the Reasoning: When LLM Agents Decide to Follow Prompt Injections
items.summary: arXiv:2610.24048v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM agents that read untrusted content can be hijacked by prompt injections. Runtime monitors that try to catch a hijack before the agent acts, and benchmarks that score each task with a single run, share an assumption: whether an agent follows an injection is settled when the injection is read. We test this assumption with branching rollouts that replay an episode exactly up to the step at which the agent reads an injection and then resample the rest of the episode many times, splitting the outcome variance into a part fixed at read time and a part decided afterwards. Across four AgentDojo suites, a Qwen3 agent without thinking is largely decided at read time (0.91 of the outcome variance lies between states); with thinking on, this share drops to 0.62 (95% CI of the drop [-0.38, -0.22]), in the same direction for three attack templates and two success labels. How much is fixed at read time is a property of the model that the same measurement reveals, and thinking lowers the attack success rate of Qwen3 but raises it for two other models. Resampling from reasoning prefixes shows that the decision forms gradually as the agent reasons. Zero-shot chain-of-thought monitors built on cheaper models miss much of what is already decided, whereas stronger monitors, and a lookahead monitor that judges simulated next actions, come close to what the prefix determines. Finally, single-run labels of thinking agents disagree with a rerun up to 35% of the time, so benchmarks need repeated runs per task.

items.summary: arXiv:2610.24087v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Can large language model (LLM) agents deliver expert-level operations research (OR) solutions directly from original client materials, without prior expert reformulation? Hidden evaluation checks feasibility and compares objective quality against original expert solutions accepted by clients before benchmark construction. Deployment-Adjusted Quality (DAQ) averages expert-relative quality across instances, assigning zero to infeasible deliveries. Across 11 frontier LLMs using coding-agent harnesses, several exceed the expert reference in conditional objective quality, but none matches its DAQ; the strongest primary Claude Code configuration achieves 88.39% strict feasibility and a DAQ of 0.87 against the expert reference of 1. Client information acquisition extends beyond clarification into solution development and validation, with some later stages showing higher confirmed issue-resolution proportions. Trajectory analysis identifies formulation and implementation failures, while task-equalized research-chain completion rates range from 24% to 45% across models on evaluable tasks. items.summary: arXiv:2610.24157v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present CoDA, an open-source human-LM collaborative codebook development assistant that helps domain experts develop annotation guidelines for annotating new variables in unstructured text with language models. In practice, developing these codebooks is time-consuming and challenging, particularly for concepts that require expert knowledge. CoDA addresses this gap by collaborating with domain experts to iteratively develop codebooks through targeted review of incorrect language model predictions and incorporating expert feedback into the evolving codebook. We demonstrate CoDA on two real-world case studies: extracting health indicators from homelessness case management notes and classifying sentiment of wildlife trafficking posts on social media. Across both domains, CoDA produces codebooks that achieve downstream classification performance comparable to expert codebooks while reducing codebook development time from several weeks to two hours and requiring 5X fewer manually annotated examples. Applying CoDA to generate annotations at scale, we identified 2,410 case notes that contained health discussions or referrals and 10,196 social media posts expressing negative sentiment that may warrant investigation for potential wildlife trafficking. By accelerating codebook development, CoDA helps practitioners use language models to extract domain-specific insights from unstructured text at scale.

items.summary: arXiv:2610.24236v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) improves the reasoning capabilities of large language models, but often reduces the diversity of their reasoning behaviors. We study this phenomenon from the perspective of finite-sample learning dynamics and show that limited on-policy rollouts can progressively suppress semantically distinct but equally rewarded reasoning modes. Once a mode becomes sufficiently under-sampled, standard on-policy RLVR rarely recovers it. Motivated by this observation, we propose TAR, a Targeted Adaptive Replay framework that preserves diverse correct reasoning behaviors already present in the base policy. TAR constructs a compact memory bank of diverse base-model solutions and selectively replays them through an adaptive mechanism that activates only when stored behaviors are being suppressed during RLVR. Across six mathematical reasoning benchmarks and two Qwen2.5 model scales, TAR consistently achieves a better balance between reasoning performance and diversity preservation than existing diversity-preserving post-training methods, while substantially reducing the forgetting of correct base-model solutions. items.title: When Do Repetition Loops Lock? Truncation Sampling, Bounded Penalties, and a Blind Spot in DRY
items.summary: arXiv:2610.24715v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Language models sometimes repeat verbatim until the generation limit. We study the exit rather than the entrance: given that a span has already been repeated $n$ times, when is escape still possible? Along the loop the context is deterministic, so loop survival under any sampler can be computed exactly from one forward pass. Pure sampling leaves a positive escape probability at every step; top-$p$ with threshold $\pi>1/2$ locks a position exactly when the continuation probability reaches $\pi$. A bounded penalty can leave a position locked; a penalty that outgrows the model's preference for the loop over unseen tokens guarantees escape under top-$p$. The same analysis predicts a blind spot in the widely deployed DRY sampler: its sequence breakers cap the penalty at $\lambda b^{g-1-a}$ for loops whose longest breaker-free run has $g$ tokens. On eleven open models, 66\% of locked units with $g=6$ stay locked under DRY and 1\% with $g=8$. In free generation with llama.cpp, all 109 loops that survive DRY have $g\le 7$. We propose DRY-C, which adds a term that grows exponentially with the number of verbatim recurrences, up to its look-back window. With it, none of 720 structured-output generations looped to the length limit, and task completion stayed close to DRY's.

items.title: DiffuPlan: Editable Planning State for Diffusion Language Model Agents
items.summary: arXiv:2610.24717v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Diffusion language models (dLLMs) are emerging as an alternative to autoregressive (AR) language models, yet dLLM agents largely inherit an interaction protocol designed for AR generation: once intermediate state is written, later observations can only be incorporated by appending more text. We ask whether this capability can support a different agent-state paradigm in which intermediate planning state is directly revisable as evidence arrives. We introduce DiffuPlan, a diffusion search agent that maintains a single editable planning state and reconstructs only the affected steps when later evidence resolves an entity or changes the search route. items.title: Who Gets Unmasked? Sampler-Induced Bias in Diffusion Language Models
items.summary: arXiv:2610.24795v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Diffusion language models (dLLMs) generate by gradually unmasking a canvas, so their samplers decide not only which token to write but also when to commit it. Common commit rules, including LLaDA's default, commit the positions whose sampled tokens are most probable; this peeking favors majority options. To separate the sampler from the model, we read the model's belief about a fork, such as a protagonist's gender, in one forward pass, and show that this belief matches exact sampling from the model. Measured against it, peeking samplers on LLaDA and Dream amplify occupational gender stereotypes and collapse opinion distributions, and confidence-based ordering shifts gender-balanced occupations toward men, more so under faster parallel decoding. We propose Fork-First Sampling, which decides the fork before anything else is written: it follows the belief or any target distribution, improves fluency, and avoids the stories that remark on the protagonist's gender, which prompt-based fixes produce, at the cost of one forward pass. items.title: Efficiency Measured in English: Tokeniser Coverage Bounds Small Language Models on Indic Scripts
items.summary: arXiv:2610.24818v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Small Language Models with quantisation and parameter-efficient adaptation are widely offered as the route to multilingual AI under compute constraints, and their efficiency is almost always reported as a single memory figure. Its vocabulary contains 0% of Odia's codepoints, 1% of Telugu's and 2% of Kannada's, and for five of eleven scripts the measured fertility sits at the UTF-8 byte-fallback ceiling, on Odia at 99.6% of it, with 93.6% of emitted tokens being raw bytes. Because SentencePiece byte fallback never raises an unknown-token marker, this failure is entirely silent: TinyLlama's UNK rate is 0.0% on every script, including the one it reads as bytes. We further show that low fertility can indicate the opposite of efficiency: mBERT posts its best score anywhere (1.10 tokens/word, on Odia) while discarding 87.9% of the text as UNK. MuRIL, an Indic-vocabulary encoder with a fifth of TinyLlama's parameters, reads every script at 1.23-2.26 tokens/word with zero UNK and zero byte fallback. items.title: Measuring Data Diversity with Embeddings: A Taxonomy and Benchmark for Diversity Measures
items.summary: arXiv:2610.24888v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Diversity is a critical property of text corpora, with direct implications for training data curation, test set design, and model generalization. items.title: How Well Can LLMs Verbalize Mathematical Formulas? A Multi-Domain Evaluation

items.title: What Can't Jev Decide? Probing the Limits of One-Pass Decision Models

On a benchmark that varies one factor at a time, Jev finds and selects records without error up to 20k tokens and 64 options, but once the answer depends on two or more updates of one user, accuracy falls, to 53-80% at sixteen updates, because similar records interfere. On real decision items graded by how many thinking tokens a reference LLM needs, Jev answers 97.5% of the items that one forward pass of that LLM solves, but only 74% of the others. Jev also does not know its limit: its confidence flags the errors it makes itself but not those it inherits from a stale input, and neither an explicit nor a trained hand-off option catches the latter. The open models we evaluate share these limits. Checking the state such models rely on requires a model that reasons.

The proposed approaches detail various features that can be extracted from the subgraphs and reranking models to select the most probable answers from a list of candidates. Experiments were conducted on Wikidata to evaluate the effectiveness of the proposed approaches. This involved enumerating all the main feature types that can be extracted from mined subgraphs and a detailed analysis of the proposed features and reranking method combinations. items.title: RARE: Reinforcement Learning with Adaptive Rubric Evolution for Open-Ended Generation
items.summary: arXiv:2610.25434v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Verifiable rewards have advanced reinforcement learning in mathematics and code. However, many valuable open-ended tasks share three properties: no automatic verifier of overall quality, multiple requirements to satisfy jointly, and multiple valid responses to each query. Training therefore needs feedback on requirement satisfaction across different valid responses. Rubric-based reinforcement learning provides this feedback by aggregating scores from explicit criteria. As learning progresses unevenly, some criteria become fully satisfied and lose discrimination while others remain informative. Dynamic methods revise shared rubrics or select evolving criteria to restore discrimination, but may also change useful criteria. To address this, we propose Reinforcement Learning with Adaptive Rubric Evolution (RARE). The core idea is to use current policy feedback to guide both which criteria change and what their replacements assess. Sample-level updates replace criteria fully satisfied across current outputs with checks of remaining quality differences, retaining all other criteria and scores. Within this rule, we compare rewarding desirable qualities with penalizing observed flaws. Video script generation exemplifies these properties and supports content production. Its demands for coherent, executable narratives under constraints make it a challenging testbed. Targeting flaws performs best across three video types with a mean gain of 3.82 points over matched static rubrics. Model and human preferences support these gains. Improvements also extend to writing and general generation benchmarks.

items.title: DiaLong: Benchmarking Reminiscence in Long-Context Dialogues

We present DiaLong, a long-context dialogue dataset and accompanying memory task that standardizes evaluation in this space. It consists of 100 unique conversations created by humans and then augmented with LLMs, extending beyond lengths found in existing datasets. Our selected memory task is fact recall: classify 40 candidate facts about a dialogue as true or false. This task directly probes the model's ability to actively retain and retrieve information, serving as a critical measure of memory within extended conversational contexts. In testing both the latest LLMs and proposed memory enhancements on DiaLong, we demonstrate that more work needs to be done to enable LLMs with better memory performance. By enhancing memory capabilities, LLMs can improve in maintaining coherence, relevance, and human-like interaction over extended conversation. items.title: Cognitive Map in Large Language Models
items.summary: arXiv:2610.25596v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: It has long been proposed that animals construct cognitive maps to support flexible behavior in novel environments. We tested whether large language models form similar representations using relational reasoning tasks and causal "mosaic experiments" that manipulate internal activations in open-weight language models. Models beyond the ten-billion-parameter scale successfully inferred unstated relationships between entities and generalized to synthetic entity names. Across model and task families, models generated abstract representations of relational structure and combined them additively with representations of entity identity, binding entities to roles within that structure. Models stored observed relationships as pairwise links that they composed retrospectively when queried, rather than prospectively positioning each entity in a global coordinate system. Binding was mediated by a sparse, distributed set of key--value pairs; by perturbing these pairs, we implanted "false memories" that altered model behavior in predictable ways. Overall, our findings reveal an internal organization analogous to a cognitive map that explains how language models reason with limited information.

items.title: MapSteal: Map-based Autonomous Knowledge Stealing Attack Against Large Language Models
items.summary: arXiv:2610.25626v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Knowledge acquisition from black-box large language models (LLMs) offers a practical approach to adapting smaller student models. Starting from a small set of initial roots, MapSteal represents acquisition targets using structured states and recursively expands them through teacher-proposed directions. Question realization, proposal admission, and deduplication constrain the acquisition process, while root-aware scheduling organizes exploration under a fixed QA budget. The resulting question--answer pairs are used to adapt student models without requiring student feedback during acquisition. Experiments with Qwen3.5 students at 2B, 4B, and 9B scales show competitive downstream performance across six medical and cybersecurity benchmarks. On the 4B medical evaluation, Full MapSteal improves average accuracy by 1.17 percentage points over a simplified recursive acquisition variant. Cross-domain evaluations show that gains depend on the domain and evaluation panel. These results demonstrate the feasibility of structured, student-independent recursive acquisition while highlighting the distinction between generating acquisition targets and obtaining useful training supervision. items.title: No Matter Who You Are: Addressivity and Sycophancy in Large Language Models
items.summary: arXiv:2610.25728v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Sycophancy, where an LLM becomes overly agreeable, deferential, or flattering toward the user, has been identified as a major failure mode. We hypothesize that the accompanying pressure to follow the addressee's instructions and align with their preferences links this addressivity to sycophancy. To test this, we use Sparse Autoencoders to extract addressivity directions from pre-trained and post-trained models and examine their relationship with sycophancy. Steering models with addressivity directions can amplify or suppress sycophancy, and this effect is observed only in post-trained models. Furthermore, comparing the internal mechanisms of both model types confirms that the association between addressivity and sycophancy is strengthened through post-training. Finally, through a controlled post-training experiment, we find that models are sycophantic not toward a specific addressee but toward any recognized addressee, suggesting that the presence of an addressee, rather than the addressee's identity, is what elicits sycophancy.

items.title: Where RL Breaks: Localizing and Repairing Failures via Targeted Continued Pretraining
items.summary: arXiv:2610.25836v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) is widely used to improve reasoning in language models, yet growing evidence suggests that it mostly sharpens what the base model can already do. We look inside the RL policy's own rollouts and find that failures are localized: whether a rollout fails is strongly predicted by a small set of characteristic n-grams, ranging from reflection phrases such as "let's recheck" to specific operations such as "the inverse of A". These failures persist throughout RL training, although they are not beyond the model's reach: other sampled answers to the same question are often correct. Building on this observation, we use the failure $n$-grams to retrieve text from the pretraining corpus and continue pretraining the base model on it before RL. The resulting corpus has only 35M tokens, 3--4 orders of magnitude smaller than typical mid-training. We evaluate this approach on OLMo2 and Qwen3 models trained with RL on (1) GSM8K; (2) a mixture of math, commonsense, and knowledge questions; and (3) general math and science reasoning. Despite its size, the corpus yields consistent gains: our approach outperforms continued pretraining on the same amount of text sampled from the pretraining corpus across 10 out of 11 settings, including by $2.0$ points on GSM8K when inserted before mid-training. The retrieved text also transfers across model families: text retrieved for OLMo2-1B's failures improves Qwen3-4B on the mixture by $1.9$ points over the same baseline. Together, our results suggest that where RL fails is a cheap and effective signal for selecting pretraining data.

items.title: Learning to Reason Efficiently with Interventional Step Credit
items.summary: arXiv:2610.25876v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large reasoning models often produce lengthy chain-of-thought (CoT) traces mixing useful intermediate steps with unnecessary ones. Despite their effectiveness, such signals reflect the model's behavior at a step rather than that step's contribution to the answer. To address this, we propose the interventional step credit (ISC), which takes a causal-intervention view and assesses step importance to the reasoning through targeted parameter-level interventions. Building on ISC, we further propose IGPO, which uses ISC to guide fine-grained advantage rescaling in reinforcement learning, reducing redundant steps while preserving the important ones. items.title: MITRA-lexicon: Lexica of attested translations from Sanskrit into English, Tibetan and Chinese

We evaluate the lexica against reference dictionaries and manually corrected gold alignments. items.title: AdaExploreBench: Benchmarking LLM Agents for Proactive Exploration and Test-time Adaptation in Evolving Environments
items.summary: arXiv:2610.25950v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) agents are increasingly deployed in unfamiliar and evolving environments, requiring them to proactively explore, understand, and adapt to environmental dynamics. However, existing benchmarks rarely test whether agents can proactively discover how an environment works and adapt as it evolves. To address this gap, we introduce AdaExploreBench, a benchmark for proactive exploration and test-time adaptation in evolving environments. By instantiating environmental dynamics as hidden rules, AdaExploreBench requires agents to actively acquire evidence and infer the rules. Under implicit rule drift, the latent rule changes without announcement, requiring agents to detect from degraded performance that prior knowledge is stale and re-explore. Experiments on eight leading LLMs show that proactive and adaptive exploration remain challenging: GPT-6 Sol achieves only 61.9% calibrated accuracy, while providing sufficient evidence or removing rule drift improves average performance significantly by close to 10%. These results reveal a critical bottleneck in current LLM agents: they can often reason effectively from informative evidence once it is available, but struggle to actively acquire the right evidence and recognize when previously acquired evidence is no longer valid.

items.title: TempoMoE: Identifying and Steering Fast-Slow Thinking Experts for Efficient Multimodal Reasoning
items.summary: arXiv:2610.25999v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multimodal Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) reasoning models rely on long chain-of-thought (CoT) for complex tasks, yet often overthink easy inputs, increasing token cost and latency, and sometimes degrading accuracy. Existing methods optimize reasoning length during training or impose external control at inference, but leave the underlying reasoning mechanism a black box. We find that fast and slow thinking exhibit distinct expert-routing patterns: holding the input fixed and varying only the prompted reasoning tempo produces stable routing shifts. Suppressing slow-thinking experts shortens the reasoning chain, whereas suppressing fast-thinking experts lengthens it, providing causal evidence that these experts influence reasoning depth. Based on this finding, we propose TempoMoE, a training-free, two-stage framework. It identifies fast- and slow-thinking experts via tempo-contrastive routing analysis and redistributes routing weights within the original top-k set according to sample difficulty. It amplifies fast-thinking experts and suppresses slow-thinking experts on easy inputs and reverses this adjustment on hard ones, enabling difficulty-adaptive control over reasoning depth. We evaluate TempoMoE on Kimi-VL, Qwen3-VL, and ERNIE-4.5-VL across six benchmarks. Compared with Vanilla, TempoMoE consistently improves accuracy while reducing output tokens, with accuracy gains of up to 2.6 points and token reductions of up to 35.4%.

items.title: Accelerated Drift of Scientific Prose in the LLM Era: Evidence from an Interrupted Time-Series Analysis
items.summary: arXiv:2610.26008v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Every scientific text is embedded in the writing norms of its time: it reflects earlier publications while also shaping the texts that follow. The growing use of LLM-based writing tools introduces a new factor in this evolving system, but the linguistic changes coinciding with their emergence remain insufficiently understood. We compare pre- and post-2022 trajectories across vocabulary, punctuation, readability, and syntax in abstracts from arXiv's artificial intelligence, statistics, and quantitative biology categories and from medRxiv. Using interrupted time-series regression, we find substantial post-2022 changes across multiple feature families and research domains, including increases in average word length, reduced formula-based readability, and declines in maximum dependency-tree depth and sentence-level depth variation. Individual features follow different dynamics: some lexical markers accelerate persistently, while others rise and then recede. Our findings show that isolated marker frequencies capture only part of the shift: changes in the rate, direction, and structure of linguistic trajectories provide complementary evidence of broader post-2022 change in scientific-preprint writing. More broadly, these findings motivate monitoring scientific writing as a multidimensional, evolving system rather than through a fixed set of LLM-associated markers.

items.summary: arXiv:2610.26416v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) is particularly well suited to code generation because generated programs can be objectively evaluated through execution. Our results do not support either hypothesis under the configuration tested. Although co-evolution improves training performance, these gains do not generalize to held-out problems. Compared at the same stage of training, rollout recycling produces roughly 34x greater KL divergence from the reference policy than execution-only GRPO. Over training, trained tokens per GRPO sequence fall from 185 to 86 as training pass rate increases, while held-out performance declines or fails to sustain early gains. We characterize these patterns as single-adapter policy drift: the shared trainable parameters increasingly depart from pretrained code-generation behavior without corresponding gains in generalization. The results show that higher training reward alone is not evidence of generalizable code self-improvement and highlight the importance of held-out evaluation and drift diagnostics.

items.title: Mitigating Reward Hacking in Preference Reward Models with Evolving Penalties
items.summary: arXiv:2610.26496v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reinforcement learning for language models has moved from preference reward models to verifiable rewards, which sustain much longer optimization. We introduce Dynalize, which mitigates reward hacking online, during policy training. Periodically and asynchronously, a language model analyzes training rollouts and writes penalties for undesirable behaviors that the reward model appears to reward; a judge applies them to every rollout. In clinical counseling and creative writing, training on the reward model alone raises its score continuously but ultimately leads to a decline in external benchmarks. Dynalize sustains longer training and results in improved downstream performance. For example, we find that our method suppresses patterns incentivized by preference models that, without penalties, spread to most responses, and even to the model's reasoning, which the reward model does not explicitly score. Furthermore, we show that its gains hold in multi-turn training, and even after we retrain the reward model on the discovered behaviors.

items.title: Hierarchical Token Merging with Recursive Autoencoders for Unsupervised Grammar Induction
items.summary: arXiv:2610.26695v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Hierarchical abstraction is a fundamental principle across many data modalities, enabling complex sequences to be represented compositionally at multiple levels. Learning such hierarchies directly from data, without explicit structural supervision, remains a central challenge in representation learning. We investigate whether meaningful hierarchical structure can emerge from compression alone. While autoencoders learn compressed representations through reconstruction, this objective does not necessarily favour meaningful compositional structure. We study this challenge through unsupervised grammar induction, where the underlying hierarchy can be evaluated explicitly. We introduce a hierarchical token-merging autoencoder that recursively combines adjacent tokens into increasingly abstract representations, compressing entire sequences through a variational information bottleneck. The model jointly learns representations and hierarchical structure by marginalising over possible binary trees using dynamic programming. To address training instability, we combine independently trained models through unsupervised consensus and distillation. Experiments on a synthetic, ambiguous grammar demonstrate the emergence of meaningful hierarchical structure without structural supervision. The resulting model achieves 93% grammatical parse-validity and 93% exact reconstruction on held-out sequences, compared with 42% parse-validity for the strongest trivial baseline. These findings establish a proof of concept for hierarchical token merging as a mechanism for unsupervised structure discovery and abstraction learning.

However, accurately assessing speaker attribute bias in a given ASR system requires the availability of a bias evaluation dataset with comparable speech across subgroups of a speaker attribute. The dataset comprises 9 hours of speech with 3928 utterances recorded by 80 speakers for Bemba, while the Nyanja set includes 6260 utterances with approximately 18 hours of speech recorded by 127 speakers. The results of our baseline experiments demonstrate that the datasets are useful for examining gender and speaker-type attribute bias in the target languages.

items.title: MemT-1.0: Towards Memory-Native Evolution
items.summary: arXiv:2610.26825v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Memory-native evolution requires making memory an intrinsic capability of foundation models, enabling them to continuously accumulate and utilize information. To this end, we introduce MemT-1.0, a new architecture of memory foundation models that internalize memory as part of model computation. Building on Metis, MemT-1.0 employs Gated DeltaNet-2 with a stable token-level memory update mechanism within each turn. We further introduce Mixture-of-Storage to scale native memory capacity. Following a deliberate backbone preparation, we develop a two-stage training pipeline consisting of continued pre-training and post-training, supported by 34B tokens of training data and efficient training and inference infrastructure. We release a model family comprising MemT-1.0-Nano and MemT-1.0-Flash, and conduct a comprehensive evaluation of memory and general capabilities. The results show that they outperform the parametric memory baselines on average and remain competitive with retrieval-augmented methods, while largely preserving general capabilities. At a history length of 128K tokens, MemT-1.0-Nano achieves approximately $1.86\times$ end-to-end inference speedup and a $66\times$ reduction in persistent storage relative to full context KV cache. By internalizing retrieved procedural experience, MemT-1.0 improves task success on agentic tasks, providing a practical step toward memory-native evolution.

items.title: RefCraft: Benchmarking Visual-Reference-Conditioned Agentic Generation through Web Development
items.summary: arXiv:2610.26826v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Beyond basic tool use and coding skills, effectively incorporating visual references into agentic generation is equally essential for applying AI agents to real-world productivity tasks. We study this crucial capability through webpage development, a practical and readily evaluable setting in which existing benchmarks remain largely idealized: they typically focus on reconstructing visual targets or generating webpages from textual instructions alone, overlooking the more common workflow of developing from visual examples. Specifically, we introduce RefCraft, a benchmark comprising 300 realistic multimodal webpage-development tasks that combine natural-language instructions with screenshots from one to five reference webpages. Agents must selectively interpret and utilize these references while rendering, visually inspecting, and iteratively refining their outputs. We evaluate the resulting open-ended artifacts using independently verifiable keypoints and complementary programmatic and VLM judges. Across nine frontier (M)LLMs, the strongest system achieves an overall score of only 52.12 out of 100, revealing that visual-reference-conditioned agentic generation remains a substantial challenge for current models in practical webpage-development settings.

items.title: LatComm: Reusable Context Compression for Latent Communication between Large Language Models
items.summary: arXiv:2610.26840v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Systems that combine several large language models (LLMs) often use one context for many questions. When the context is passed between models as text, the receiving model processes all of its tokens again for every question. Avoiding this cost requires a context representation that is compact, reusable across questions, and readable by a different LLM. Existing compression and latent communication methods each provide only some of these properties. We introduce LatComm, a Latent Communication interface that provides all three by separating encoding from reading: the context is encoded once without the question, and the receiver selects what to read for each question. A frozen context encoder LLM compresses the context into a fixed-size packet and sends it to a different frozen receiver LLM, which reads the packet through cross-attention, with gates computed from its prompt. On 12 multiple-choice question-answering datasets, LatComm improves average accuracy over single-vector baselines by up to 10.2 points. On QuALITY, it reduces the receiver's input by 57x and answers the questions of an article 3x faster.

items.title: Multi-LLM Systems Exhibit Robust Semantic Collapse
items.summary: arXiv:2605.17193v3 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Whether machines can originate novel content has been debated for nearly two centuries, from Lovelace's assertion that no engine can "originate anything" to Turing's question of whether a machine can amplify ideas brought in from outside. Interacting multi-LLM systems, increasingly deployed for autonomous generation, reopen this question empirically. Here we show that such systems exhibit semantic collapse, systematic convergence in semantic representations despite apparent lexical variation, with no retraining or weight updates. The pattern holds across model families and over 200 to 1,000 rounds. Thirteen intervention implementations tested, spanning decoding parameters, prompt design, agent composition, activation engineering, and reinforcement learning, did not reliably restore semantic diversity. Mechanistic analyses suggest that semantic collapse is not solely attributable to the alignment or conformity biases examined here, but is consistent with intrinsic properties of autoregressive generation. Our results point to persistent constraints on the ability of multi-LLM systems to sustain open-ended exploration in closed-loop settings.

items.title: GardenBench: A lightweight, daily evaluation of LLM capabilities

This allows us to compare the accuracy and features of responses across model providers and versions. We account for daily variations in model accuracy, capturing both model progress and degradation, for instance, when a model is changed post-deployment or when a new model is released. We base our evaluation on general-use tasks and make our results publicly accessible via a live dashboard, diversifying existing approaches to LLM testing. items.title: Latent Multimodal Memory Reasoning
items.summary: arXiv:2610.23890v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Long-term personalized agents are required to reason over distributed history across modalities and evolving dialogue states. While existing flat cross-modal methods compress visual evidence prematurely and struggle with temporally stale observations, they neglect the necessity to unify multimodal and cross-session evidence. Crucially, raw multimodal memories are inherently entangled and heterogeneous, making fine-grained visual grounding and cross-modal reasoning computationally prohibitive. To this end, we present latent multimodal memory reasoning, i.e., LMMR, a novel neuro-symbolic framework that shifts long-term multimodal memory organization into a continuous latent space. Specifically, (i) instead of converting images to text and relying on static retrieval, LMMR maps both textual hidden states and visual patch features into a shared Sparse Autoencoder concept space, establishing sparse activations as common semantic addresses to dynamically construct a turn-level multimodal memory graph. (ii) A graph encoder then aggregates cross-modal and temporal dependencies across the task-specific latent subgraph, injecting the graph readout as a continuous residual rollout into the generation backbone while retaining native visual tokens to preserve fine-grained details. Extensive experiments on nine Mem-Gallery tasks and twelve MemEye settings demonstrate that LMMR significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in capturing complex multimodal dependencies while enabling faithful and grounded responses.

items.title: How Data Scales in Agentic Reinforcement Learning: Laws and Synthesis Strategies
items.summary: arXiv:2610.23946v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Pretraining scaling laws treat training data as a one-dimensional quantity: a token count. Agentic reinforcement learning (RL) inherits this scalar abstraction, but modern synthesis pipelines now generate \textit{tasks}, \textit{environments}, and \textit{trajectories} independently and at very different costs, turning data into a structured design space. This raises a question pretraining never had to answer: given a synthesis budget, \textit{which axis} should be scaled? We address this question end-to-end with three tightly coupled contributions. First, we decompose agentic data into three cardinality axes (task, environment, trajectory), plus a reward-density control variable, and fit per-axis scaling relations on different large language models (LLMs) across math+code, SWE, web, and UI/tool application domains. Across all model sizes, model families, domains, and RL algorithms (PPO and GRPO) we measured, the scaling exponents order as environment $>$ task $>$ trajectory. When environment diversity is decomposed into world and environment-structure diversity, its advantage is mainly driven by the former, while the latter is just comparable to the task diversity. Second, we use the fitted laws as a common ruler to price synthesis methods, capturing each method's efficiency as a per-axis discount factor and identifying critical synthetic-to-real ratios at which collapse begins; these ratios differ by an order of magnitude across axes. Third, we cast budget allocation as a constrained optimization under our laws and discounts, deriving a Chinchilla-style compute-optimal recipe and validating it at held-out scale. The empirical results demonstrate that following the recipe yields up to $1.7\times$ compute efficiency over the dominant ``scale-the-trajectories'' practice.

items.title: UltraData-Code: From Raw Repositories to Algorithmically Dense and Task-Oriented Code Data
items.summary: arXiv:2610.23960v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Code generation has become a core capability of large language models (LLMs), and code data is central to the pre-training process that develops it. As obtaining public code of sufficient quality becomes more difficult, further progress cannot rely on corpus expansion alone. Tiered data management instead applies increasingly targeted processing to smaller data pools, producing data states suited to different training objectives. Following this perspective, we present UltraData-Code as four connected data states spanning repository archival at L0, standardized natural code at L1, algorithmic selection at L2, and task-oriented synthesis at L3. L0 preserves repository data and provenance for reprocessing, while L1 applies scalable filtering, normalization, and near-deduplication for broad pre-training. L2 selects high-quality algorithmically relevant files using language-adaptive relevance signals and quality constraints, yielding approximately 400B tokens of UltraData-Code-L2 across 11 programming languages for focused continual pre-training. L3 converts selected implementations into structured programming exercises, yielding approximately 150B tokens of UltraData-Code-L3 across the same 11 languages for task-oriented mid-training or supervised fine-tuning (SFT). Under controlled 10B-token continual pre-training of a 1B model, L2 improves pass@1 over L1 by 7.80 percentage points (pp) on EvalPlus and 5.13pp on MultiPL-E. Replacing half of the L2 training tokens with L3 yields a further gain of 8.42pp and 8.07pp on the two benchmarks, respectively. Both gains increase when the training budget scales to 100B tokens. We have released our datasets and classifiers to support further research on LLMs.

items.title: LLM Evolution in a Simple Simulated Market
items.summary: arXiv:2610.24033v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Arguments that AI systems will evolve in harmful ways are largely made in the abstract. We provide a concrete empirical example. We simulate simple markets consisting of populations of twenty Large Language Model agents tasked with solving arithmetic problems. Agents differ only in their system prompt; those that go bankrupt are removed and replaced by mutated copies of the prompts of successful agents. Two market conditions select for opposite phenotypes: a market that rewards accuracy produces agents with high accuracy (94%) and high token use; a market that charges per token produces agents with low accuracy (10%) and low token use. In the second market, only tokens are incentivised yet we see a collapse in accuracy. Token use and accuracy are correlated traits such that selection on one also moves the other, and behaviour adapts along an unpriced dimension. A third neutral condition with no selection allows us to separate these effects from bias in the mutation operator. Adaptation occurs through a collective optimisation process that operates above the level of individual agents, who are never told the payment rule, do not receive feedback, and have no memory.

items.title: LogicVal:A Logic-Formalized Benchmark for Constraint Satisfaction in Text-to-Image Generation
items.summary: arXiv:2610.24051v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Text-to-Image (T2I) generative models have made significant progress in producing high-fidelity images from natural-language prompts. Alongside this progress, numerous benchmarks have been developed to evaluate capabilities such as attribute binding, numeracy, spatial reasoning, and commonsense reasoning. In this work, we propose a new perspective on T2I evaluation by casting it as a constraint-satisfaction problem. We introduce a logical framework that formally specifies the benchmark domain, including objects, attributes, and relations, alongside the constraints that generated images must satisfy. We evaluated four state-of-the-art T2I models across 9 classes of constraints ranging from a single-object-attribute to multi-object relationships constraints involving logical operators ($\forall, \exists, count, \rightarrow$). Our results reveal a substantial gap between single-object and complex conditional multi-object relationship constraint classes, with the best-performing model achieving 98% accuracy on the former and just 53% on the latter. We assess compositional generalisation, finding that the best-performing model`s accuracy drops from 84% on single-constraint prompts to 20% when satisfying multiple constraints simultaneously. Identifying unsatisfiable constraints is also challenging, with the best model correctly recognizing only 23% of such prompts. Building on this framework, we introduce \textbf{LogicVal}, an evaluation methodology that combines neural visual detection with logical reasoning to assess constraint satisfaction in generated images. On CLEVR, LogicVal achieves ROC-AUC scores ranging from 0.88 to 0.98, indicating strong alignment with human judgments. These findings underscore the value of logic-based evaluation for characterizing T2I model capabilities and limitations.

items.title: World of SWECraft: Agent Collaboration at Scale via Simulated Software Worlds
items.summary: arXiv:2610.24061v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As teams of AI agents take on larger projects and long-standing open problems, agent collaboration offers another dimension for scaling inference-time compute. To understand what makes such collaboration effective and scalable, we develop Software World, a framework for simulating multi-agent coworking in realistic software ecosystems. It comes with a pipeline to create environments of real, interdependent Python packages of different topics, sizes, and dependency structures, which we call software worlds. In a simulation, agents maintain packages in the world with a high-level goal of improving software efficiency, and they are free to discover tasks to work on and collaborate with others. We evaluate agents' work in a world collectively by measuring speedup in hidden dependent packages. The framework allows us to study different elements of collaboration by varying communication, ownership, and resource allocation. We run simulations in three different worlds, totaling more than 10,000 hours of agent work across eight models. Overall, performance improvement scales with inference-time compute, with the best model improving downstream efficiency by up to 31%. We show that most agents can find meaningful tasks via collaboration, but some frontier models can prematurely stop looking for improvements and make little progress. We release the simulation framework and traces to support future studies of agent collaboration at https://szj.io/sw.

items.title: Location, Location, Generation: Where You Ask Matters for Generative Engine Optimization
items.summary: arXiv:2610.24081v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Generative search engines answer local and commercial questions with a written answer and a few cited sources. A growing practice of generative engine optimization (GEO) monitors which sources and brands these answers show, typically from a single place. In this paper, we present a controlled audit of how the user's location changes the sources that generative engines cite. We ask 300 questions of ChatGPT with 19 declared locations, and of ChatGPT and Gemini from five network locations, each twice to measure run-to-run noise (31,200 answers). The engines take location from different channels. ChatGPT follows the location an application declares, down to the city: it writes the place into its own searches, and its search backend localizes results even when the queries name no place. It ignores the network. Gemini ignores the declared location and follows the country of the network, changing most of its sources even for questions that do not depend on place. The businesses the answers recommend change with the sources. Thus, visibility in generative search is specific to the user's location, and audits must control both channels.

items.title: Cache2LoRA: Understanding and Improving Context Internalization
items.summary: arXiv:2610.24107v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Context-to-LoRA methods encode documents as low-rank parameter updates, allowing language models to answer without retaining the source text in their decoding context. How reliably do these updates preserve facts and support their use under different instructions? Controlled diagnosis of existing context-to-LoRA methods separates fact discrimination, target retention, and response adaptation. Competing sources influence answers, while target-only construction and memory-state optimization improve recovery at fixed update size. Recovering facts also does not ensure that answers follow response instructions. We introduce Cache2LoRA, which uses each query to aggregate evidence from a reusable frozen document cache before generating LoRA updates. Trainable encoding operates only on the query and memory-token suffix, and multi-style supervision teaches both evidence preservation and answer expression. Across 17 tasks, Cache2LoRA improves on existing context-to-LoRA methods and achieves macro F1 of 0.663, approaching full-context in-context learning at 0.671. For 32K documents and 256-token outputs at batch size 16, its decoding throughput is 5.9$\times$ that of full-context ICL. At matched memory size, generated LoRA preserves answer accuracy more reliably than the learned-KV variant under long, diverse intervening text and combines more effectively with retained document KV, yielding higher hybrid F1 and EM.

items.title: Joint, Decoupled, or Agent: When Each Multimodal Alignment Paradigm Wins
items.summary: arXiv:2610.24108v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Jointly pretrained multimodal encoders are a common way to combine modalities, while alternatives integrate their information during downstream training or inference. When does each approach win? We compare three paradigms, instantiated with public checkpoints, across 16 paired datasets in five domains and multiple training-label budgets. JOINT trains a fusion head on frozen, jointly pretrained encoders. DECOUPLED trains a fusion head on frozen, independently pretrained encoders. AGENT gives a frozen LLM task instructions, labelled examples, available sample text, and supervised unimodal readouts. No paradigm dominates the complete 144 dataset-budget combinations: DECOUPLED wins 54, JOINT 44, and AGENT 46 by mean utility. ScienceQA, MELD, and MetMeme shift from AGENT to fusion as supervision increases. Between the fusion paradigms, JOINT leads on four of five QA datasets across all evaluated budgets, while higher unimodal 5-NN accuracy is associated with a relative shift toward DECOUPLED across eight classification datasets (Spearman $\rho=-0.67$). We test whether representation and task diagnostics predict these preferences on held-out datasets before fitting their candidate systems. A two-step cascade combines these diagnostics with task and budget metadata to select AGENT or fusion, then JOINT or DECOUPLED. Under leave-one-group-out evaluation, it selects the winner in 71.4% of cells versus 54.2% for metadata-only routing, with mean relative regret 0.028 versus 0.057. Using geometry, supervised representation diagnostics, and text-label matching together yields higher accuracy and lower regret than using any one of these sources with metadata. These results connect paradigm preferences to supervision budget, task format, and unimodal 5-NN accuracy. items.title: Inside the Loop: A Mechanistic Study of Weight-Tied Transformers on Depth-Bound Algorithmic Tasks
items.summary: arXiv:2610.24135v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Solving algorithmic tasks with many sequential steps typically requires scaling up transformer depth or chain-of-thought length, incurring unfavorable parameter and inference-compute costs, respectively. Looped transformers, which reuse one block of layers across many iterations, are poised to address this, since they scale effective depth without adding parameters or tokens. Yet, it remains unclear what each iteration is actually computing, or whether the loop merely simulates a deeper untied stack. Here, we study directed permutation traversal, in which a model follows $H$ hops from a starting node and reports the node it reaches, so every intermediate hop has a known ground truth. We find that a minimum effective depth is necessary to solve the task, beyond which the degree of weight tying becomes the determining factor. For instance, a looped transformer with a four-layer block iterated eight times solves the task in every seed, while an identically-trained untied transformer of the same effective depth never does, succeeding only with a lower learning rate or supervision of its intermediate layers. Probing and intervening on the residual stream, we find that the looped model advances through the intermediate nodes gradually, forming a staircase that adapts to its iteration budget, whereas the untied model, at that lower rate, exposes them only in its final layers. Taken together, our results recast looped transformers as iterative program learners, which allocate their iterations to successive steps of the algorithm and solve tasks that identically-trained untied models of the same effective depth do not. Code is available at https://github.com/magnus-sesodia/insidetheloop.
