items.title: Reducing double-dipping in single-cell topic models with three-way count splitting
items.summary: arXiv:2610.24130v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Topic models learn gene programs from single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) data, and the same counts are then used to test which genes and donors are associated with those programs. Count splitting is the standard remedy for this reuse, but it has not been tested when an encoder reads each cell's counts. On a 104,400-cell lupus cohort with 300 permuted null genes per run, naive tests rejected 36% of null gene-topic pairs at a nominal 5% level, and the usual two-way split rejected 38%, because the encoder sees the tested gene's own held-out count. Encoding topic usage on a separate third of the counts, with beta-binomial thinning, lowered this to 7.7% (6.7% for genes outside the model); for two other models, LDVAE and scETM, the rate was 7.0-7.3% (naive 51-59%). A label-free interferon program shifts in held-out counts in the lupus cohort and in a pre-specified COVID-19 cohort, and donor-level topic usage predicts disease (AUROC 0.96) beyond cell-type proportions (0.86 and 0.58 in the two cohorts). Calibration and prediction did not depend on the model. We do not claim better clustering, prediction or topic stability. Code, figures and result tables are public (MIT license; DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23307193).

items.title: Sequence-to-Sequence Neural Surrogate Modeling of Transient Responses in High-Speed Links with Variable Design Parameters
items.summary: arXiv:2610.24141v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: This paper presents sequence-to-sequence (seq2seq) neural surrogates for high-speed transient response modeling and signal integrity analysis in fixed and variable design parameter spaces. To identify the structural requirements for prediction accuracy, multiple neural architectures were evaluated with respect to different training strategies such as sample-based and unit interval-based, as well as input configurations such as TX-only and TX+RX. For fixed design parameters, feedforward neural networks achieve accuracy comparable to recurrent models while requiring lower computational cost, as the static mapping can be approximated by fully connected and non-sequential representations. Variable design parameters alter the electromagnetic characteristics of the interconnect, which creates parameter-dependent temporal dynamics that require sequence-aware architectures to resolve the evolving interactions within the transient response. The results based on a 14-dimensional variable design parameter scenario show that while autoregressive TX+RX feedback suffers from severe phase drift and error propagation under variable conditions, non-autoregressive TX-only inference leads to stability. To overcome the structural limitations of standard decoders, a recurrent Early Fusion LSTM is proposed, which injects design parameters at the initial encoding stage. This approach achieves superior prediction accuracy, with an RMSE of 31.0 mV and an R2 of 99.51% for transient waveform prediction, an RMSE of 30.7 mV and an R2 of 99.57% for eye-height prediction, and an RMSE of 19.5 ps and an R2 of 99.94% for eye-width prediction. These results demonstrate that neural seq2seq surrogates are accurate for transient response modeling and signal integrity analysis in complex variable design parameter spaces.

items.title: Candidate-dependent residual routing trades top-of-list accuracy for recall in sequential recommendation
items.summary: arXiv:2610.24200v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Candidate-dependent routing lets a sequential recommender weight a user's past behaviors differently for each item it scores. We test whether this flexibility helps by adding a small residual routing module to a self-attentive baseline, in two versions that differ only in what sets the routing weights: the user's history representation or the candidate item's embedding. Across five paired seeds on the REES46 cosmetics-shop dataset, with matched training for all three models, candidate-dependent routing leaves the primary metric, normalized discounted cumulative gain at cutoff ten (NDCG@10), essentially unchanged (mean relative change +0.003%). Secondary and exploratory analyses show that this flat average hides two effects that cancel. The candidate-dependent model places more relevant items in its top ten (recall +1.81%) but ranks the first one lower (mean reciprocal rank -1.09%), and most of its new hits land at positions six to ten. Its gains come from queries with at least one target among the user's last 50 events, while queries whose targets all lie outside that window get worse. In this form, candidate-dependent routing trades accuracy at the top of the list for recall further down.

items.title: Certified neural approximations for parabolic obstacle problems
items.summary: arXiv:2610.24202v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Residual-trained neural surrogates carry no error guarantee, a limitation for free-boundary problems such as phase change and contact. We derive guaranteed error bounds for neural approximations of parabolic obstacle problems in first-order state--flux--multiplier form. The main result bounds the flux error of the network and the energy error of its feasible projection $\max\{v,g\}$ by the constitutive residual, the initial mismatch, the complementarity defect, and the PDE residual weighted by $c_F^2/\alpha$, without the coercivity and norm-equivalence constants of the first-order formulation. It extends the Apushkinskaya--Repin majorant for the heat operator to general coefficients, free multipliers and a flux bound. A penetration-consistency result shows that neural triples with arbitrarily small bound exist. Outward-rounded cellwise Taylor-model enclosures turn the bound into a finite computation valid on any adaptive partition. The flux and gradient errors of the projected output are certified below $0.27$ and $0.33$ of the solution scale for a one-dimensional Stefan problem and, after adaptive refinement, below one half for all three trained networks on a two-dimensional expanding disk. On an expanding ellipse the gradient bound stays above one half; substitution diagnostics trace the floor of the trained networks to the projected state near the free boundary, and the remaining gap to enclosure overhead. Without a closed-form solution, a validated lower bound replaces the solution norm; there the enclosure is nearly exact, but the trained networks have errors above the solution scale and no useful accuracy is certified. The bounds control a state--flux norm, not the multiplier or the free-boundary location.

items.title: Censored Flow Matching for Synthetic Time-to-Event Generation
items.summary: arXiv:2610.24233v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Generating time-to-event data is increasingly important in survival analysis, but it remains statistically challenging because event times are often censored and thus prevent flexible generative modeling. To fill this gap, we propose a novel method called censored flow matching (CFM), aiming at providing a flexible flow-based generative mechanism for synthesizing time-to-event data as well as learning their corresponding probabilistic densities. Unlike existing methods, CFM does not rely on survival likelihoods to handle censoring, but instead exploits the monotonicity property of differential flows to address censoring via pullback sampling. Under this framework, we implement an alternating procedure between pullback sampling and CFM steps, leading to a flow-based expectation--maximization (EM) algorithm tailored for time-to-event inference. Under mild distributional conditions, we establish the convergence of CFM to the true event-time distribution as the EM iterations proceed. We then apply CFM to generate time-to-event data and estimate their probabilistic densities, where the observed censoring time can be incorporated to provide truncated sampling or truncated density estimation for survival inference. Through extensive simulation studies, we demonstrate the benefits of CFM for complex and large-scale data generation. Finally, we apply CFM to analyze data from the Organ Procurement and Transplantation Network (OPTN) and the Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care IV (MIMIC-IV), showcasing its benefits for synthetic and predictive survival analyses in terms of data fidelity, predictive performance, and empirical privacy characteristics.

items.title: Extending Myerson's Optimal Auctions to Correlated Bidders via Neural Network Interpolation
items.summary: arXiv:2610.24240v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We aim to design revenue-maximizing single-item auctions that are deterministic, strategy-proof, and ex post individually rational --- the quintessential fundamental model for optimal mechanism design. While Myerson's seminal work solved this model for independent bidders, straightforward extensions to correlated settings often result in non-monotonic, and therefore non-strategy-proof allocations. Critically, optimal allocation design for correlated bidders is NP-hard to approximate, rendering theoretical optimality guarantees in this domain computationally intractable. We establish a new standard of empirical rigor for this theoretically hard model by proposing an empirical pipeline. We synthesize neural interpolation of Myerson's greedy allocation based on marginal profits (the correlated variant of virtual valuation), formal neural verification to enforce exact strategy-proofness, and a constructive repair procedure. Empirically, our method is highly effective, consistently achieves near-optimal revenue across a wide range of distributions, including synthetic, adversarial, and real-world (consumer, financial, and industrial) datasets. Compared to existing manual and neural baselines, our approach shows substantial improvement, often reducing the revenue gap by an order of magnitude. Our study is also the first to introduce (unattainable) greedy revenue as a rigorous upper bound for empirical benchmarking, providing a definitive quantitative performance measure where true optima remain theoretically elusive. We demonstrate the generality of our approach by extending it to multi-unit auctions with unit demand and integrating our verification techniques into RegretNet to achieve exact strategy-proofness.

items.title: CoCoNet: Convex Conformal Network for Multi-Dimensional Uncertainty Regions
items.summary: arXiv:2610.24246v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Conformal prediction (CP) provides distribution-free coverage guarantees under exchangeability, but the efficiency of its prediction regions depends critically on the choice of the conformity score. This is particularly important in multivariate regression, where dependencies across output dimensions induce complex joint uncertainty structures. This paper introduces CoCoNet (Convex Conformal Network) for learning convex conformity scores that induce flexible, data-adaptive prediction regions. CoCoNet learns the score from held-out data by optimizing prediction-region efficiency while enforcing convexity with respect to the residual. CoCoNet then applies split-conformal calibration to retain finite-sample coverage guarantees. The paper presents two variants of the method: CoCoNet$_{\mathrm{Spline}}$, based on piecewise-linear scores, and CoCoNet$_{\mathrm{ICNN}}$, based on Input Convex Neural Networks. Experiments compare CoCoNet with other CP baselines over synthetic and real-world datasets with output dimensions ranging from 2 to 16. The results demonstrate the flexibility of CoCoNet in learning different response types. Across 8 models and 30 multi-dimensional regression tasks, CoCoNet$_\text{ICNN}$ and CoCoNet$_{\mathrm{Spline}\text{-}\ell_1}$ achieve the best efficiencies with average ranks of 1.45 and 2.75, respectively. In particular, CoCoNet$_\text{ICNN}$ ranks first on 22 tasks out of 30 in terms of efficiency.

items.title: Blackbox Performance Analysis of LLM-based Network Control
items.summary: arXiv:2610.24348v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: LLMs are becoming an indispensable part of network control systems due to their impressive reasoning. Before such LLM-enabled systems can be deployed, it is imperative to develop tools that can audit their performance on previously unseen inputs. However, auditing these systems is challenging due to the inherent opacity of LLMs. LENS is the first step towards black-box performance analysis of LLM-enabled network control systems. It uses novel methods to extend deep reinforcement learning to guide the search for performance gaps and inputs that make LLMs struggle. LENS finds large gaps for LLM-based traffic engineering and GPU allocation systems, and even matches existing white-box analyzers designed for hand-crafted TE heuristics.

items.title: Can Agents Keep Secrets They Were Never Told? Benchmarking Latent Privacy Risks Across Sessions with MemJoin
items.summary: arXiv:2610.24359v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: To support sustained interactions and personalized assistance, agents use long-term memory to retain and combine user information across sessions. Reusing such memories can lead an agent to state a sensitive relation while completing an ordinary task that does not require it. The relation to protect and the combination of clues that reveal it may remain hidden at memory write time, when later records and tasks are still unknown. In this paper, we introduce MemJoin, a privacy benchmark of 288 synthetic analysis cases in which the complete history entails a sensitive relation, but every individual session is insufficient. We evaluate six memory systems with the same answer-generating model, alongside full-history and no-history controls. Each system writes and updates memories in session order and later retrieves context for an ordinary task, while target annotations remain with the evaluator. We separately check which target attribute values appear in stored records and retrieved context, and whether the final answer states the complete, person-linked relation. In a separate paired test on a prespecified subset, removing shared identifiers and other connecting clues can change complete-relation output while all checked target attribute values remain visible. These findings show why checking attribute visibility alone is insufficient to evaluate what records from different sessions reveal together.

items.title: Learning from the Right Regions: Class-Conditioned Explanation Guidance for Medical Imaging
items.summary: arXiv:2610.24381v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Deep neural networks can achieve strong predictive performance in medical imaging while relying on regions unrelated to the predicted finding. Explanation-guided learning can address this problem, but multi-label classification introduces a key challenge: multiple abnormalities may coexist in an image, requiring each prediction to align with its corresponding spatial evidence. We propose a class-conditioned explanation-guided learning framework that constructs a separate explanation for each positive class and penalizes evidence outside its class-specific annotated regions. We instantiate the framework using Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping (Grad-CAM) and evaluate it on 14 abnormalities using EfficientNet-B1, ViT-B/16, ViT-B/32, and Swin-B. Explanation guidance substantially improves annotation alignment across all architectures: All-Saliency Precision increases from 0.140 to 0.625, 0.052 to 0.551, 0.060 to 0.403, and 0.095 to 0.570, respectively. These improvements are accompanied by smaller, architecture-dependent changes in classification performance. Our results show that class-conditioned explanation guidance can substantially improve where multi-label classifiers concentrate their explanatory evidence while largely preserving predictive performance.

items.title: A decomposition-integration framework coupling singular spectrum analysis with a volatility-adaptive LSTM for stock price forecasting
items.summary: arXiv:2610.24384v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Financial time series exhibit multi-scale, high-noise, and non-stationary volatility dynamics. Decomposition--integration frameworks built on complete ensemble empirical mode decomposition with adaptive noise (CEEMDAN) have advanced this field, yet existing CEEMDAN hybrids remain unstable: high-frequency mode mixing contaminates downstream predictors, and the heterogeneous volatility of decomposed components is not matched by any volatility-adaptive mechanism. To address these gaps, this paper proposes CEEMDAN-SE-SSA-VMGL. CEEMDAN adaptively decomposes the original series, and sample-entropy-driven K-means clustering groups the intrinsic mode functions into high-, mid-, and low-frequency and residual components. Singular spectrum analysis (SSA) is then applied to the high-frequency group, whose singular-value decomposition of the trajectory matrix and principal-component reconstruction decouple intertwined pseudo-oscillatory modes and alleviate mode mixing. We further design a plug-and-play robust LSTM variant, the volatility-modulated GARCH-LSTM (VMGL), which embeds a differentiable GARCH(1,1) layer inside the LSTM cell as a risk gate; the estimated conditional volatility multiplicatively scales the forget-gate activation, letting memory decay adapt to the instantaneous volatility while remaining fully end-to-end trainable. Component predictions are linearly combined. On five US and Chinese financial series (CSI 300, CSI 500, AAPL, GOOGL, S&P 500), the proposed model is compared with eleven benchmark architectures, lowering the forecasting error by 9% to 24% relative to the best benchmark and by 60% to 70% relative to a standard LSTM. Diebold--Mariano and model-confidence-set (MCS) tests confirm the statistical significance and stability of the gains, spectral analyses verify the SSA denoising efficacy, and backtesting demonstrates the framework's economic utility.

items.title: Learning volatility-adaptive forgetting via GARCH-modulated LSTM for stock price forecasting
items.summary: arXiv:2610.24386v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Stock price forecasting is hindered by the heteroscedastic nature of financial time series, in which turbulent and tranquil regimes alternate. Although the Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) network is widely used for this task, its gates are oblivious to such volatility variation, so memory retention remains fixed regardless of market conditions. A common remedy is to supply volatility estimates as an additional input feature, yet this leaves the internal memory dynamics untouched. Instead, volatility can serve as a direct regulatory signal over the gate activation itself. This paper presents the Gsigmoid-LSTM model, which embeds Generalized Autoregressive Conditional Heteroscedasticity (GARCH(1,1))-derived volatility estimates into the LSTM forgetting gate through the Gsigmoid activation function, a volatility-adaptive variant of the sigmoid that combines a volatility adjustment factor with slope regulation via a learnable parameter. The model thereby automatically prioritizes recent information during turbulent periods while preserving long-term dependencies in stable markets. In the engineering application of daily stock price forecasting, extensive experiments, including activation function comparisons, baseline evaluations, and ablation studies, demonstrate that this structural gating modification effectively improves forecasting accuracy and robustness. The proposed model significantly outperforms a feature-level fusion baseline carrying the same volatility signal on all five datasets, as confirmed by Diebold-Mariano tests with all p<0.01, attains the best average rank of 1.00 in the Friedman test across nine models, and achieves the lowest MSE and MAE on all five datasets.

items.title: Prototype-Guided Optimization of Quantum Data Embeddings with Linear Cost
items.summary: arXiv:2610.24403v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In supervised quantum machine learning with classical data, classification performance critically depends on the geometry induced by quantum data embedding. Existing data-adaptive approaches rely on pairwise fidelity evaluations between samples, which scale as $O(B^2)$ for $B$ samples and create a computational bottleneck in iterative embedding optimization. To address this issue, we propose a prototype-guided framework for efficient data-adaptive quantum embedding. Using class-prototype separation and sample-to-prototype compactness, we derive a measurable lower certificate for class-ensemble distinguishability and construct a prototype-based objective requiring only $O(B)$ fidelity evaluations. We integrate this objective into an end-to-end pipeline that combines task-specific quantum circuit architecture optimization with continuous refinement of the data-embedding parameters. Across five benchmark datasets with up to 20 qubits, our method retains competitive quantum kernel support vector machine (SVM) performance while reducing fidelity-evaluation cost, with particularly strong gains over budget-matched pairwise optimization on T-MNIST. Geometric analyses examine how the learned embeddings relate to kernel alignment and classification margins, revealing dataset-dependent benefits and limitations. We further derive a prototype-based classifier in the reproducing kernel Hilbert space that provides an explicit witness for the SVM objective and a low-cost proxy for model selection, and extend the framework to multiple prototypes for multimodal class structures.

items.title: Margin-Based Generalization for Quantum Machine Learning with Classical Data Encoding
items.summary: arXiv:2610.24426v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Understanding generalization is essential for assessing the practical viability of quantum machine learning. In many applications, quantum models operate on classical data that must first be encoded into quantum states, making the encoding part of the effective hypothesis class. We develop a margin-based generalization framework for this setting, covering both fixed and trainable quantum data encodings. For fixed encodings, the existing margin bound transfers unchanged. For trainable encodings, we derive a bound using a two-scale covering argument that combines the original margin-dependent term with an additive encoding-capacity term of order $\tilde O(\sqrt{L/m})$, where $L$ is the number of trainable encoding parameters and $m$ is the training-sample size. Across 19,440 simulated training runs spanning various image datasets, circuit architectures, and optimization settings, the inverse margin performs best among five baseline and two bound-derived complexity measures under conditional-independence and 90th-percentile sign-error criteria, within bootstrap uncertainty. These results provide a unified margin-based view of generalization in quantum machine learning with classical data.

items.title: Private Evaluation of High-Dimensional Functions
items.summary: arXiv:2610.24477v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study differentially private black-box evaluation of arbitrary high-dimensional functions. Given a dataset $S$ and query access to a function $f$---whose sensitivity may be unknown or unbounded---the goal is to privately output an approximation to $f(S)$. The black-box evaluator can only query the value of $f$ over a down neighborhood of $S$ (i.e., those subsets of $S$ that are obtained by removing a bounded number of elements from $S$). We design generic black-box evaluators for both pure and approximate differential privacy through a reduction to high-dimensional private quasi-concave optimization (QCO). Our black-box evaluator enjoys a geometric notion of utility. Consider the vectors obtained by applying $f$ on sets in a down neighborhood of $S$. With high probability, the evaluator's output is guaranteed to be in the convex hull of these vectors. Our work generalizes the result of Linder et al. [LRSS25] for real-valued function evaluation to high dimensions. It also recovers the private center-point guarantees of Beimel et al. [BMNS19], with an explicit additive approximation to maximum Tukey depth. We also apply our evaluators to user-level quasi-concave and convex optimization, showing how they can improve upon the sample-and-aggregate baseline of Nissim et al. [NRS07] by replacing the multiplicative data overhead with an additive overhead. Finally, we show that our formulation of high dimensional black-box evaluation and high dimensional private QCO are equivalent up to a factor of the dimension: the hardest private evaluation instances already arise from the cases that $f$ is a (non-private) quasi-concave optimizer.

items.title: Denoising Implicit Variational Inference
items.summary: arXiv:2610.24509v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Semi-implicit variational inference (SIVI) expands the representational capacity of variational families, but optimizing the Evidence Lower Bound (ELBO) remains challenging because the marginal score of the semi-implicit distribution is generally intractable. Unbiased Implicit Variational Inference (UIVI) and related methods address this difficulty through reparameterized ELBO gradients, but existing approaches estimate the required score indirectly through reverse-conditional sampling or approximation, which can be computationally costly and unstable. We propose Denoising Implicit Variational Inference (DIVI), which learns the marginal score directly via denoising score matching. The learned score is used as a plug-in estimator in the pathwise ELBO gradient, replacing inner reverse-conditional sampling with a score-network evaluation. We analyze DIVI as inexact stochastic gradient ascent and show, under stated assumptions, that the averaged stationarity measure is controlled by the usual optimization term and the average score-matching error. Empirically, we evaluate DIVI on both synthetic distributions and a variety of real-data Bayesian inference tasks. The results show that DIVI improves over the current UIVI baselines while reducing the cost of ELBO-gradient estimation.

items.summary: arXiv:2610.24525v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Real-time control of tokamak plasmas requires the electron density profile. The surrogate enables realtime-compatible gradient-based reconstruction and uncertainty quantification from the reflectometry and interferometry measurements. We compare four uncertainty quantification methods - multi-seed ensembles, the Laplace approximation, Metropolis-Hastings, and a Gaussian method independent of the reconstruction fit. The resulting uncertainty is scored with CRPS and coverage calibration, separately on the observed and unobserved regions. We further demonstrate advantage of our approach over standard analytical function fit on synthetic and experimental DIII-D discharges.

items.title: Write Once, Query Many: Evolving Compact Reusable Memory for Long Videos
items.summary: arXiv:2610.24537v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Long videos often exceed the context capacity of multimodal large language models (MLLMs), while agentic search repeats costly video processing and grounding for each query. Reusable memory can amortize this cost, but must preserve information for questions unknown during construction. We propose Video-EMem, an evolvable video memory harness built on time-anchored perceptual observations. This representation combines compact free-form text with sparse images to preserve semantic content and complementary visual details across temporal scales, supporting temporal navigation without a fixed semantic schema. A Writer encodes each video once by consolidating overlapping multiscale observations, and a Reader retrieves and organizes evidence solely from the resulting memory. With the underlying models frozen, we evolve their workflows and operators using distinct feedback: query-independent source fidelity and coverage for the Writer, and QA failures in evidence localization and utilization for the Reader. Experiments support this separation for generalization beyond development queries, with our evolution strategy improving average accuracy by 7.2% over the unevolved harness. While reducing storage by about 99.86% on average relative to raw videos, Video-EMem improves Qwen3-VL-30B by an average of 2.6% across three long-video QA benchmarks over direct input of 2,048 frames. Using the same o3 answer model as the state-of-the-art agentic method, it improves average accuracy by 2.5% with lower per-query latency.

items.title: Accelerating Finite-Sum Bilevel Optimization with Fully First-Order Oracles
items.summary: arXiv:2610.24538v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study nonconvex--strongly-convex bilevel optimization with finite-sum objectives and fully first-order oracles. We propose Sampled Implicit Corrections for Bilevel Optimization (SICBO), which combines a penalty approximation with variance-reduced corrections for the lower-level variables. Under componentwise lower strong convexity, SICBO finds a point $x$ satisfying $\mathbb{E}\|\nabla\Phi(x)\|^2\le\varepsilon^2$ within $\tilde{O}(N+\sqrt{N}\kappa^{7/2}\varepsilon^{-2})$ component-gradient calls, where $N$ is the total number of components and $\kappa$ is the normalized lower-level condition number. The bound achieves square-root finite-sum dependence using only gradients and preserves the best known deterministic fully first-order condition-number exponent for smooth problems. Our improvement follows from a curvature-dependent bound for nonlinear correction errors, which permits epochs of length $\tilde{\Theta}(\sqrt{N/\kappa})$ with batches of size $\tilde{\Theta}(\sqrt{N\kappa})$. A single-level reduction shows that the dependence on $N$ and $\varepsilon$ is optimal up to logarithmic factors for fixed $\kappa$.

items.title: Conditional Weight of Evidence for Gradient-Boosted Credit Models: Estimation, Additivity and Its Relation to Adverse Action Reasons
items.summary: arXiv:2610.24586v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Traditional weight of evidence assigns a credit characteristic a value based on its association with default across a population. Credit analysis also requires an assessment of that characteristic in the context of an individual applicant's record. We study conditional weight of evidence for this purpose. It measures the change in default log odds from observing a characteristic after the remaining credit information is known. Its sign identifies whether the characteristic adds adverse or favorable information for that applicant, and its magnitude measures the strength of that information. The same characteristic value can therefore receive different assessments for applicants with different payment histories or other credit attributes. We develop estimators using gradient-boosted trees and evaluate their accuracy in a bureau-style simulation. Regressions of the full model's predicted probabilities recover conditional evidence more accurately than separate models fitted to default outcomes, provided the full model is accurate. They also recover a deliberately constructed file-age effect whose direction varies with utilization and is often missed by marginal weight of evidence. Local class-frequency estimates improve on marginal weight of evidence but remain inaccurate for some weak effects. An application to FICO HELOC data illustrates estimation when the population evidence is unknown. Conditional weight of evidence provides an applicant-specific interpretation of the information in a credit characteristic; its population summary, a conditional information value, splits the joint information in the record across blocks when averaged over orderings. Neither is an adverse action reason, which explains the fitted score difference between the applicant and chosen passing records.

items.title: Modeling Uncertainty Propagation in 3D Morphable Models
items.summary: arXiv:2610.24646v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study the problem of mapping parameter-space variance of a 3D Morphable Model (3DMM) to per-vertex variance. Traditionally, per-vertex variance has been used to visually interpret the learnt parameter uncertainty. However, mapping parameter-space variance to per-vertex using sampling or error propagation is computationally expensive. We address this limitation with Closed-form Local Uncertainty Estimation (CLUE), which transforms the parameter-space distribution of 3DMMs to per-vertex through a closed-form approximation. CLUE emerges from applying the law of total variance to the 3DMM formulation and is modular, computationally inexpensive, and accurate. Subsequently, we study integrating CLUE for in-the-wild human mesh recovery training and inference. We note that CLUE uses the geometry of the mesh as an inductive bias when predicting the variance, leading to improved accuracy. Through extensive qualitative and quantitative experiments, we show that when used in training, CLUE (1) outpeforms probabilistic and deterministic baselines on metrics evaluating joints, mesh and uncertainty, and (2) has the highest uncertainty-to-error spearman correlation, with applications including data mining and interpretable uncertainty. Finally, we share SAM 3D Body (CLUE) which augments the regressor with high resolution uncertainty maps. We make our code available at https://github.com/vita-epfl/CLUE

items.title: Lightweight Machine Learning for Classifying Disaster-Related Social Media Posts
items.summary: arXiv:2610.24652v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Classifying disaster-related social-media posts into humanitarian information labels is challenging because individual messages are typically short and context-limited, humanitarian categories can overlap semantically, and the CrisisBench label distribution is strongly imbalanced. This study investigates whether lightweight lexical machine-learning methods can provide effective and computationally efficient classification under these conditions. Using the CrisisBench v1.0 English humanitarian task, comprising 87,455 records across predefined Train, Development and Test splits, we conduct a controlled comparison of TF-IDF representations and lightweight classifiers, with Macro-F1 as the primary model-selection metric. Beyond aggregate predictive performance, the study jointly examines per-label behaviour, directional error patterns, relative decision margins, computational requirements, and the effect of domain-specific training through a tropical-cyclone specialist model. The selected balanced LinearSVC with unigram-bigram TF-IDF and C=0.5 achieved an Accuracy of 0.8282, a Macro-F1 of 0.6578 and a Weighted-F1 of 0.8315 on the held-out Test split. Lower decision margins were substantially associated with prediction errors, while the tropical-cyclone specialist achieved modestly higher in-domain aggregate performance with substantially lower feature and fitting requirements. The study contributes a controlled, label-sensitive and resource-aware evaluation of lightweight humanitarian text classification that characterises not only aggregate performance, but also where these models fail and how their behaviour changes under domain-specific training.

items.title: Knowledge Diversion: A Novel Paradigm for Pre-training Decomposable Image Generation Models
items.summary: arXiv:2610.24664v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Large-scale pre-trained models have become foundational to modern machine learning, yet conventional pre-training objectives primarily optimize source-domain performance without explicitly considering downstream requirements. Consequently, transferable and task-specific knowledge remains entangled within a shared parameter space, limiting selective knowledge reuse and efficient downstream adaptation. This limitation is particularly consequential for image-generation models, which must accommodate diverse conditions and domains. To address this challenge, we introduce Knowledge Diversion (KDiv), a condition-aware pre-training paradigm for learning inherently decomposable generative models. Before pre-training, KDiv factorizes randomly initialized weights into rank-one Knowledge Units, which are organized into learngenes and tailors. During pre-training, continuous condition-aware routing consolidates knowledge shared across conditions in learngenes while directing condition-dependent variations to tailors. This structured organization enables learngenes to capture transferable generative priors and tailors to develop condition-specific expertise, allowing the resulting model to be selectively recombined for diverse downstream conditions. Extensive experiments across class-, text-, and image-conditioned generation demonstrate that KDiv consistently matches or surpasses dense baselines at comparable pre-training cost and achieves the strongest average downstream performance with a trainable parameter budget comparable to low-rank adaptation methods.

items.title: Geometry-Aware Interpolation for Inverse Problems
items.summary: arXiv:2610.24687v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Recovering missing visual information from incomplete or degraded images remains a challenging problem, particularly when spatial variations and complex image structures affect reconstruction accuracy. Although Spatial Transformer Networks (STNs) facilitate spatial feature alignment, their reliance on conventional linear or bilinear interpolation limits their ability to capture the underlying geometric characteristics of image data. Furthermore, interpolation based on a restricted set of neighbouring pixels can introduce inconsistencies in gradient propagation, potentially affecting optimisation stability. To address these limitations, we propose a Geometry-Aware Interpolation Network (GAIN), a variational autoencoder-based framework that incorporates manifold geometry into spatial transformation and image reconstruction. Rather than estimating pixel intensities solely from fixed spatial neighbours, GAIN exploits the local tangent structure of the data manifold to construct geometry-informed intensity approximations. An entropy-based regularisation mechanism further guides the estimation of spatial transformation parameters, promoting more adaptive interpolation. In addition, a convolutional normalisation strategy is introduced to regulate the magnitude of non-zero activations and improve gradient stability during training. Extensive experiments on challenging image completion and classification benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of GAIN in improving predictive accuracy while reducing computational cost compared with existing methods.

items.title: Martingale Posterior Cox Processes
items.summary: arXiv:2610.24787v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Cox processes provide a principled Bayesian nonparametric framework for modeling event-based data through an underlying intensity function. However, existing inference methods for estimating the intensity typically rely on computationally expensive Markov chain Monte Carlo sampling or approximate inference techniques. In addition, to ensure tractability, these methods often define priors over indirect latent structures, making them challenging to interpret. In this paper, we introduce the Martingale Posterior Cox Process (MPCP), which recasts Bayesian intensity estimation as inference over unobserved events given the observed event history. This perspective avoids the need to define complex priors while retaining the flexibility of nonparametric modeling. We propose a scalable, GPU-friendly copula-based predictive update, and provide strong theoretical guarantees for the convergence of the predictive resampling algorithm. Empirically, we show that MPCP provides excellent performance in both simulations and real data at a fraction of the computational cost of competing Bayesian approaches.

items.title: Is User Calibration Still Necessary for Continuous Myoelectric Control? A Closed-Loop Comparison of Calibration-Free Controllers
items.summary: arXiv:2610.24802v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The need for user-specific calibration remains an often-cited barrier to widespread adoption of myoelectric control. Cross-user models trained on large multi-user datasets can now recognize gestures from unseen users without calibration, but they have been evaluated almost exclusively offline, leaving open whether calibration is still needed in closed-loop control. This study compared six calibration-free controllers, trained on 306 users of the EMG-EPN-612 dataset and used without any calibration data from the test participant, against three calibrated controllers in a closed-loop Fitts' law target-acquisition task with sixteen participants. The calibrated controllers achieved higher offline balanced accuracy (90.6% against 73.1% for the best controller of each paradigm), but completion rates did not differ significantly between paradigms, and the highest completion rate was achieved by a calibration-free controller. Calibrated controllers moved faster on successful acquisitions, partly because of their individually fitted speed mappings, though not significantly after correction for multiple comparisons. However, every calibration-free controller produced more direct and stable trajectories than every calibrated controller, even after adjusting for cursor speed. Offline accuracy did not predict completion rate across controllers or within participants, and across paradigms higher offline accuracy was associated with poorer trajectory quality in 15 of 16 participants. Without any calibration data from the end user, a model trained across a large population matched calibrated control in completion rate and exceeded it in trajectory quality. The offline accuracy gained through calibration should therefore not be taken as evidence of a closed-loop benefit.

items.title: Tilted Mondrian: Triage and Mitigation of Fine-grained Disparities in Conformal Prediction
items.summary: arXiv:2610.24813v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Fairness in conformal prediction is often pursued through Mondrian calibration, which provides finite-sample coverage guarantees separately across groups. These guarantees, however, are coarse: substantial disparities can remain within finer strata. This coarse-to-fine fairness issue raises two questions: how severe can such disparities be, and how can they be mitigated? Aggregate disparities can depend on how groups are distributed across strata. For severity assessment, we introduce propensity standardization to examine the effect of population composition, and show how group composition can induce disagreement between aggregate and finer-stratum comparisons. For mitigation, we develop Tilted Mondrian to improve fairness compared to group-Mondrian at a finer level without additional model training. Tilted Mondrian retains groupwise coverage guarantees and mitigates coverage and prediction set size disparities within finer strata. Finally, we derive a method-agnostic bound that quantifies how much reduction in finer-stratum coverage disparity can be achieved.

items.title: Query-Dependent Reading for Quantized Inner-Product Estimation: A Minimax Separation
items.summary: arXiv:2610.24890v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study quantization for inner-product estimation when storage and reading have separate budgets. In the static bit-probe model [Yao, 1981], an encoder stores $w$ bits about $x$ before seeing a query $y$, and a reader probes at most $r<w$ bits to estimate $x^\top y$. Both vectors lie in the $d$-dimensional Euclidean unit ball. Protocols may be randomized, and computation is unrestricted. Performance is measured by $d$ times the worst-case mean-squared error over $x,y$, averaged over protocol randomness. First, we show that query-independent reading cannot benefit from extra storage. Any such reader is equivalent to fully reading an $r$-bit message, even when later reads depend on previously returned bits. At fixed positive rates $W=w/d$ and $R=r/d$, the normalized minimax error converges to $1/(4^R-1)$, independent of $W$. The upper bound was already known [Ordentlich and Polyanskiy, 2025]. We prove the matching lower bound for arbitrary scalar decoders, extending the result for unbiased compressors [Safaryan et al., 2020]. Then, we show that query-dependent reading makes extra storage useful. We construct a two-batch protocol using Gaussian projections and random thresholds, with asymptotic normalized error at most $(\pi+o(1))/[4R\log(W/R)]$ as $W/R\to\infty$. At fixed $R$, this error vanishes as storage grows, giving an unbounded advantage over query-independent reading. We also prove a finite-dimensional lower bound for arbitrary encoders, decoders, and fully branching readers. In the doubly sparse regime $W/R\to\infty$ and $R\log(W/R)\to0$, it gives normalized error at least $(1-o(1))/[2R\log(W/R)]$. Thus, our protocol is optimal within a factor of $\pi/2$ in the leading constant.

items.title: Scalable and Adaptive Distribution Regression via Random Features
items.summary: arXiv:2610.24892v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Distribution regression seeks to learn mappings from probability distributions to response variables and has emerged as a unifying framework for kernel methods, multi-instance learning, and set-valued learning. Despite its success, kernel-based distribution regression remains computationally expensive and sensitive to kernel choice, motivating scalable and adaptive representations. Building on random feature approximations, we develop a finite-sample analysis of Random Feature Distribution Regression (RaDR) under two-stage sampling. Our perturbation analysis separates the effects of distribution-level sampling, finite within-bag sampling, and random feature approximation. We establish sufficient feature-budget conditions under which RaDR preserves the order of our excess-risk upper bound for exact two-stage kernel distribution regression while maintaining computational efficiency. We further propose Adaptive Random Feature Distribution Regression (A-RaDR), a unified score-guided framework that adaptively allocates random features according to downstream learning objectives. Experiments on synthetic benchmarks and 41 real-world datasets demonstrate that RaDR delivers substantial computational savings while maintaining competitive predictive performance, whereas A-RaDR further improves learning accuracy in distribution regression while retaining the computational speed up. Together, these results establish a practical and theoretically grounded framework for adaptive, scalable distribution learning

items.title: ATLAS: Expert-Guided Sustainable Satellite Backhaul for Off-Grid Wildlife Monitoring
items.summary: arXiv:2610.24910v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Remote wildlife monitoring increasingly depends on high-fidelity cameras and sensors deployed far from grid power and terrestrial networks. Low Earth orbit satellite links can provide connectivity in these settings, but their high power draw and variable bandwidth, combined with intermittent on-site solar harvesting, make continuous backhaul infeasible. Current systems therefore filter at the edge, with motion triggers that waste limited energy and bandwidth on environmental artifacts, or fixed vision models that cannot follow evolving expert objectives. We present \textsc{ATLAS}, an expert-guided edge-to-cloud system that treats satellite backhaul as a scarce resource for off-grid wildlife monitoring. \textsc{ATLAS} uses foundation models to compile natural-language expert intent into semantic scoring logic, combines semantic relevance with environmental and energy state, and uses a constrained reinforcement-learning scheduler to decide which clips to upload and when. As a representative case study, we deployed \textsc{ATLAS} for over six months across 18 off-grid salmon-monitoring river sites. \textsc{ATLAS} achieves a mean clip-selection accuracy of $87.4\%$, exceeding mean baseline accuracy by $26.4$ percentage points, while maintaining near-continuous operation through low-solar periods in which baselines incur 16.0\% downtime.

items.title: DF-PALM: Dynamic Fusion Prompt Learning for Audio--Language Models
items.summary: arXiv:2610.24921v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Few-shot audio classification requires audio--language models to distinguish variable acoustic events from limited labeled data. DF-PALM achieved 80.69% mean accuracy and 80.32% macro-averaged F1, exceeding PALM by 4.11 and 4.30 percentage points, respectively. Paired benchmark-level tests supported both gains after Holm correction. Across four shot settings, DF-PALM achieved the highest mean accuracy and macro-averaged F1 among the four evaluated prompt-learning methods. The gains extended to LAION-CLAP and OpenFLAM, with significant improvements over PALM in both metrics. At 50 candidate classes, operator-counted inference floating-point operations increased by 0.39% relative to PALM. These results support instance-conditioned feature-space adaptation as an effective approach to few-shot audio classification. Our code is publicly available at GitHub https://github.com/sunyulin0421/DF-PALM.

items.title: No Escape from the Quadratic Barrier: Adaptive Attacks on Linear $\ell_2$ Sketches
items.summary: arXiv:2610.25008v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Linear sketches estimate properties of high-dimensional inputs from a fixed low-dimensional projection. At constant accuracy, randomized Euclidean-norm sketches, notably the Johnson-Lindenstrauss transform, support exponentially many nonadaptive queries in sketch dimension $k$. For adaptive black-box queries, known privacy-based defenses guarantee $\widetilde{\Omega}(k^2)$ and it remained open whether stronger guarantees were possible. Prior attacks used more queries, restricted the responder, or provided weaker failure guarantees. We show that the quadratic guarantee is optimal up to logarithmic factors, even with a computationally unbounded responder that knows the matrix, attack algorithm, history, and query distributions and may change its randomized rule after every query. For every fixed hidden $A\in\mathbb{R}^{k\times n}$ with $n>40k$ and target accuracy $\alpha \in (0,1]$, our black-box attack uses $O(k+\alpha^2k^2\log(2+\alpha^2k))$ queries in $\widetilde{O}(1+\alpha^2k)$ adaptive rounds to force, with constant probability, a round in which a constant fraction of answers have $\Omega(\alpha)$ relative error. Our results clarify the limits of defending a fixed compressive linear representation by adapting the prediction rule.

items.title: Integrable building blocks for symplectic neural networks: learned-type layers, fiber-preserving layers, and what a single layer can do
items.summary: arXiv:2610.25023v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Exactly symplectic neural networks are built almost exclusively from shear maps and gain expressivity only through depth. We ask what else a single explicit symplectic layer can be. Observing that every layer in use is the exact flow of a Hamiltonian that is a function of commuting integrals, we obtain three families of layers: a learned-type layer, in which every conjugate pair is rotated, squeezed or sheared by a state-dependent amount and the type is found by training; moving-plane shears, residual symplectic maps outside the known ridge-function class; and fiber-preserving layers, which combine an unconstrained point transformation with a fiber translation at the cost of one linear solve. We characterize residual symplectic layers $x \mapsto x + J\nabla H(x)$: in one degree of freedom they are exactly the shears along a line, while from two degrees of freedom on a strictly larger class exists. Conjugating a learned-type layer by a symplectic network yields an exact one-parameter group with an exactly conserved learned Hamiltonian. In experiments on sixteen systems with one to forty degrees of freedom, against SympNets, H\'enonNets and learned-plane shear networks, layers built on nonlinear integrals are far more accurate when the Hamiltonian contains functions of those integrals. On nonlinear Schr\"odinger lattices with six to forty sites, twist layers alternating with linear symplectic maps are over a hundred times more accurate than every shear-based network, and with an on-site potential of learned form three to four orders of magnitude more accurate. On chains of Tao oscillators with the step size as an input, stretch layers are 45 to 70 times more accurate than learned-plane shears and recover the Hamiltonian to 1%. items.title: Normalizing Flow for Neural-Enhanced Track-Before-Detect

We introduce an environment-dependent latent intensity variable that characterizes the signal power of each object in the shared propagation environment. The probability density function of this intensity variable is represented by a normalizing flow and trained online in an unsupervised manner within the sequential Bayesian inference procedure. The learning objective is derived from a variational Bayes formulation by maximizing the evidence lower bound (ELBO), thereby accounting for the uncertainties inherent in the Bayesian TkBD problem. items.title: Non-Acceleration of the Heavy-Ball Method in 1D

Recently, the work of Goujaud et al. [Math. Program. (2025)] made progress regarding acceleration in the context of smooth, strongly convex minimization: for a small enough inverse condition number, either the method does not accelerate on quadratics, or there exists a smooth strongly convex function such that heavy-ball cycles over the roots of unity. The constructed functions have two variables, thus leaving the question of acceleration over univariate functions open. In this work, we use a Fourier-based analysis to i) provide a proof for the non-acceleration of the heavy-ball method over the class of univariate smooth strongly convex functions. We also ii) provide a strict enlargement of the previous root-of-unity cycling region, with insights regarding the "fractional" sets of Goujaud et al. items.title: Decision-Target Reversal under Informative Label Missingness
items.summary: arXiv:2610.25128v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Informative label missingness can improve classification efficiency because the pattern of label availability may itself contain information about the discriminant structure. We show that this advantage need not persist across deployment objectives: with the data-generating model and statistical experiments held fixed, informative partial classification can be favourable under one loss and unfavourable under another. We call this phenomenon decision-target reversal. For binary Gaussian discrimination, we derive a local cost-sensitive excess-risk expansion and, in one dimension, obtain explicit critical cost ratios at which the first-order risk ordering reverses. We show that the required covariance geometry arises under finite uncertainty-dependent missingness mechanisms with a fixed marginal missing-label proportion. We then extend the analysis to multiclass finite-action problems through loss-specific active-boundary curvature, yielding a general decision-target frontier. Monte Carlo experiments illustrate the predicted reversals, and a descriptive gastrointestinal-lesion application with agreement-defined label availability illustrates sensitivity to deployment costs. The results show that favourable informative missingness is a property of the statistical experiment relative to the deployment decision, rather than of the experiment alone.

items.title: Many Repairs, One Direction: Steering Code Models Toward Safer Cryptographic API Use

We introduce CrypSteer, which extracts a shared direction by normalizing repair differences and selecting a principal component aligned with repairs across misuse categories. With model weights fixed, adding one shared direction per model to its internal activations during generation improves aggregate target security rates by 5.28--15.00 percentage points over unsteered generation across languages and misuse categories. These findings connect the shared structure of cryptographic repair representations to a reusable intervention for safer code generation.

items.title: HullProbe: Measuring Interventional Part Reliance in Maritime Vessel Classifiers
items.summary: arXiv:2610.25137v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Recognizing a vessel's type from an image supports maritime surveillance and sanctions monitoring, but a classifier can reach high accuracy by leaning on the generic hull instead of the more distinctive superstructure, and is then fooled when a vessel is re-hulled or occluded. Because a surface vessel is a hull and a superstructure arranged along one axis, its parts form a 2x3 grid whose 2^6 = 64 swaps we evaluate exhaustively, and a single Walsh transform returns each part's interventional influence and its interaction spectrum. We present a unified information-geometric framework to address these issues.A wiring is a point in a probability simplex over circuits within a degree polytope. Departure from a symmetric Fat-Tree prior $\mathbf{q}$ is measured by $\DKL(\cdot \,\|\, \mathbf{q})$. The cost $U$ is the smoothed DAG critical-path length, whose gradient equals path marginals of a Gibbs distribution via forward--backward recursion.For free energy $F_{\beta_1} = U + \beta_1^{-1} \DKL(\cdot \,\|\, \mathbf{q})$, we prove well-posedness, monotonic dependence on $\beta_1$, adaptation bounds via Jeffreys divergence, and a symmetry principle for static optimality. An entropic proximal-gradient method updates multiplicatively with a $|V|$-dim dual KL projection, achieving linear convergence.For time-varying traffic, a threshold policy yields regret $O(\sqrt{\Gamma C V_1 T})$ against the switching-free optimum. Traffic changes are detected by a multinomial GLR--CUSUM detector with non-asymptotic false-alarm bounds. Multi-job generalized-mean fairness aligns with $\alpha$-fairness ($\alpha \ge 2$). Experiments on pipeline, data, and MoE workloads validate the framework against integer programming.

items.title: ChronoChart: Setup-Agnostic Channel Charting for Label-Free Indoor Localization
items.summary: arXiv:2610.25199v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Accurate radio-based indoor localization remains challenging in multipath-rich and dynamic indoor environments. Supervised fingerprinting methods achieve high positioning accuracy by learning mappings from radio channel measurements to physical locations, but require costly position labels and frequent recalibration. Channel Charting (CC) addresses this limitation by learning low-dimensional representations of Channel State Information (CSI) without position labels, yielding channel charts in which nearby points correspond to nearby physical locations. However, prominent CC methods rely on setup-specific dissimilarity metrics, such as ADP-, CIRA-, or PDR-based distances, and on precomputed $O(n^2)$ distance matrices, limiting scalability and transferability across radio systems. We propose ChronoChart, a timestamp-supervised CC framework that requires only CSI and timestamps without prior knowledge for training. Our method jointly optimizes complementary objectives: a triplet loss using temporally derived positive and negative samples to establish coarse global structure, a temporal-proximity loss that promotes smooth trajectories in the chart, and a joint-embedding loss that enforces consistency between representations of different augmentations. Evaluated on real-world 5G, MIMO, and passive UWB data, our method matches or exceeds prior CC baselines that depend on tailored distance metrics, and remains scalable and applicable across heterogeneous radio systems.

items.title: RAIL-5G: A Challenging Real-World Dataset and Benchmark for AI-Based 5G Indoor Localization
items.summary: arXiv:2610.25201v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Reliable radio-based indoor localization is essential for industrial automation, yet existing methods are often evaluated in environments that do not fully reflect the severe multipath and non-line-of-sight (NLOS) conditions encountered in real deployments. This limits our understanding of how AI, i.e., modern geometric, unsupervised, and semi-supervised localization methods generalize to industrial 5G settings. We present RAIL-5G, a public real-world 5G NR channel impulse response (CIR) benchmark recorded in an operational railway maintenance facility. RAIL-5G covers an 811m$^2$ indoor area with eight distributed radio units, robot-mounted user equipment (UE) trajectories, high-accuracy iGPS reference positions, and severe metal-induced multipath caused by train compartments and maintenance infrastructure. We benchmark geometric time-difference of arrival (TDoA), supervised fingerprinting, unsupervised channel charting, and self-supervised wireless pretraining methods. Our results highlight the difficulty of RAIL-5G: on the full dataset, TDoA reaches 7.02m mean average error (MAE), the best unsupervised method reaches 2.46m, and supervised fingerprinting achieves 0.52m. Self-supervised pretraining reduces the labeling effort by up to one order of magnitude, but the remaining gap to supervised learning shows that robust AI-based localization under severe multipath remains an open challenge. The dataset and code are available at https://iis.fraunhofer.de/rail-5g.

items.title: LiftDiff: Guided Discrete Diffusion for Quantum Code Construction
items.summary: arXiv:2610.25213v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The realization of fault-tolerant quantum computation relies on Quantum Error-Correcting Codes (QECC). Of particular interest are codes that combine a high encoding rate with sufficient distance. Existing algebraic constructions, such as lifted product (LP) codes, build a large quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) code from a classical base matrix. In this work we introduce LiftDiff, a generative approach to the discovery of QECC. A discrete denoising diffusion model is trained to generate base matrices over the group algebra $\mathbb{F}_2[\mathbb{Z}_\ell]$, which are then expanded into LP codes. The reverse diffusion process is guided by an energy function that evaluates quantum code properties, including girth, degree, sparsity and decoding performance, steering the sampler toward matrices that yield LP codes with favorable parameters. Our method discovers codes with parameters such as $[[169,13,11]]$, $[[143,15,9]]$, and $[[260,24,10]]$, including a $[[247,19,14]]$ code that achieves the highest ${kd^2}/{n}$ among the baselines. Moreover, several discovered codes outperform the Gross code across a broad range of the tested physical error rates under both code-capacity and circuit-level noise.

items.title: Estimating Causal Bounds from Observational Data With Neural Generative Models
items.summary: arXiv:2610.25246v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Identifying causal bounds from discrete observational data is a fundamental problem in causal inference. While exact analytical bounds exist for certain graphs, this is not generally the case. In this paper, we introduce a framework for estimating such bounds using neural generative models together with a new extrapolation procedure to estimate these bounds more accurately. Across multiple causal inference settings, it produces bounds that are consistently closer to the true bounds than those obtained with existing general neural approaches. We validate the framework on a range of benchmark problems for which exact bounds are available.

items.title: Persistent Representational Misalignment Induces Vision-Language Model Failures
items.summary: arXiv:2610.25252v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) fail at some tasks that are simple for humans---but why? We hypothesize that many such failures stem from VLMs' difficulties translating between vision and language representations, a misalignment the Platonic Representation Hypothesis predicts should disappear with scale. This paper is composed of two parts: in the first, we show that existing vision and language representations are linearly unalignable. This misalignment is an inherent property of the data and hence expected to persist regardless of either scale or the alignment's complexity. In the second, we demonstrate how this misalignment both leads to a predictably induced generalization failure and correlates with existing failure modes, where more representationally aligned VLM backbones accordingly exhibit fewer failures. Overall, these results imply representations will not become aligned simply given sufficient scale, providing evidence against a strong version of the Platonic Representation Hypothesis.

items.title: Federated Learning for Malware Image Classification under Data Heterogeneity
items.summary: arXiv:2610.25264v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Malware image classification (MIC), in which binary files are converted into visual representations and deep neural networks are trained to identify malware families, has recently emerged as an effective approach for malware detection. Federated learning (FL) enables malware image classifiers to be trained collaboratively by multiple clients without sharing raw data. However, a fundamental challenge in FL is data heterogeneity (non-IID), which is particularly relevant but understudied in the malware context. In this paper, we address this gap via three contributions. First, we present an empirical study of federated MIC under varying degrees of data heterogeneity across three popular malware image datasets (MalImg, Virus-MNIST, and MalNet). We show that while FL achieves strong accuracy under IID conditions, both accuracy and training stability degrade as data becomes increasingly non-IID. Second, we introduce a set of round-level statistics that characterize the data contributed by participating clients in each FL round, and demonstrate that class entropy (diversity of class labels present in a given round) exhibits strong positive correlation with global model accuracy. Third, leveraging this insight, we propose an entropy-aware client selection strategy that filters candidate client subsets based on class entropy, and show that our strategy outperforms standard random selection. Our results highlight the role of client composition in federated MIC and underscore the importance of distribution-aware classifier training under data heterogeneity.

items.title: The Explainability Illusion: Must ViTs Exhibit Patch-Decoding Interpretability?
items.summary: arXiv:2610.25289v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Transformers are widely assumed to exhibit token-decoding explainability. In particular, in vision transformer (ViT) classifiers, decoding individual patch tokens has become a common diagnostic tool due to its tendency to yield human-interpretable outputs. In light of the increasing popularity of this approach, an important question is whether token-decoding explainability is an inherent property of transformers that should be expected to hold across architectures, scales, and training objectives, or merely an artifact of some implicit bias. In this paper we systematically study token-decoding explainability across diverse ViT settings, spanning architectures, scales, and training objectives, using both controlled experiments and real-world models. We find that while some models indeed exhibit aligned and interpretable token decodings, others exhibit either inverted explainability maps or a complete lack of correlation with the image semantics. As we show, these tendencies toward different explainability behaviors are not intrinsic to the architecture and can vary arbitrarily with changes in the optimization landscape. We provide theoretical support for these observations by demonstrating a setting where a single fixed toy transformer architecture can provably implement the optimal classification rule in multiple ways, which differ in their patch-decoding explainability patterns. Our results show that token-decoding explainability is not an inherent property of trained transformers, but rather an outcome contingent on the problem setting and thus should not be a-priori assumed to hold. Code can be found in https://ronensc.github.io/Explainability-Illusion/ .

items.title: GreenNIDS: A Benchmark Workflow and Analysis Dataset for NetFlow Intrusion Detection Experiments
items.summary: arXiv:2610.25366v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Comparing the predictive performance and computational cost of flow-based intrusion detection experiments requires both quantities to be available for each run. GreenNIDS connects benchmark execution on public NetFlow datasets to a reusable analysis dataset. Model implementations write a common set of outputs, which are ingested into a run-level table with companion tables for model configuration, feature importance, and training history. The run-level table combines predictive metrics with timing, throughput, memory use, and energy estimates based on thermal design power. A CPU-only demonstration comprises 216 runs across four dataset families, three versions, and binary and multiclass tasks. Ingestion produces a 216 x 96 analysis table with no duplicate run identifiers and complete Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC) and F1 coverage. Multiclass ROC-AUC is missing for 36 PyTorch runs, making metric availability an explicit part of subsequent comparisons. The stored records support grouped performance and training-time plots, as well as resource screening after execution. Combining task-specific MCC thresholds with limits on training time, peak RAM, and estimated training energy retains 25.0% of the full run collection. These results establish compatibility within the evaluated collection and support comparisons after execution, subject to the recorded preprocessing, execution profile, and approximate energy accounting.

items.title: Whistle and Wrong Lyrics: Synthetic Queries Are Not Enough for Real-World Query-by-Melody
items.summary: arXiv:2610.25371v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: People look up a song by humming it, but also by whistling it or singing it with the wrong words. Published query-by-humming systems and benchmarks focus on hums and sung queries, and no public dataset pairs whistles or wrong-lyrics singing with song recordings. We study both query types with a melody-only retrieval system: a key-normalized pitch track embedded by a 5.2M-parameter contour encoder, with a spectral-peak tracker for whistles. First, a physics-grounded generator renders synthetic whistles and nonsense-syllable singing from the vocal melodies of 11,083 songs. Training on them raises top-1 retrieval of held-out synthetic queries against an 11,050-song gallery from 0.180 to 0.251 for whistles and from 0.193 to 0.264 for wrong-lyrics singing, but the gain does not transfer: on the MLEnd test performers the best synthetic-only model gets 210 of 339 real whistles right at top-1, against 214 for the baseline. Second, a closed-set fine-tune on real MLEnd whistles with performer-disjoint splits raises whistle-to-hum top-1 from 0.631 (95% CI 0.581-0.681) to 0.673 (0.622-0.723), on known songs only. Third, two further generations of synthetic queries also fail to transfer: melody-conditioned whistles and la-la singing from a commercial neural music model leave real-whistle top-1 at 0.631, and an open-source pipeline (YingMusic-Singer-Plus singing with partly wrong, mumbled or nonsense lyrics, a DDSP whistle synthesizer, and a melody-error model fitted on real performers) gives at best 0.619 (paired difference -0.012, 95% CI -0.038 to +0.015). Across physics-based, commercial neural and open-source neural synthetic data, nothing transferred to real whistles, which points to collecting real queries as the missing step. Code is public; models and data will be released.

items.title: TILDE: Teacher-in-the-Loop Distillation from Embodied Foundation Models
items.summary: arXiv:2610.25376v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Large-scale action pretraining equips Embodied Foundation Models (EFMs) with strong manipulation capabilities, with particular strengths in generalization and closed-loop robustness, but reproducing such pretraining requires substantial robot data and computation. We further propose AutoDAgger, an autonomous data aggregation pipeline in which a robotic reward model is utilized to monitor task progress and trigger teacher intervention, thereby collecting recovery experience without human monitoring or manual control. AutoDAgger accelerates recovery-trajectory collection by more than $2\times$ compared with the human-in-the-loop method. By unifying learning from demonstrations, on-policy teacher supervision, and teacher's corrective behavior, TILDE improves task performance by up to $4.1\times$ over behavior cloning across three real-world tasks and supports effective cross-architecture distillation.

items.title: BiDex-100: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Bimanual Dexterous Manipulation Across 100+ Simulation Tasks
items.summary: arXiv:2610.25459v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Bimanual manipulation with dexterous hands has attracted growing attention in research on robotic action models. Concretely, the benchmark comprises 106 tasks organized along five capability axes: generalization, instruction following, limited demonstrations, long horizon, and memory. Each task is paired with an out-of-domain variant featuring controlled visual and spatial changes, allowing systematic assessment of robustness. In addition, the benchmark supports two embodiments and provides 8,080 success-validated teleoperated demonstrations, totaling 6.25 million frames. We evaluate seven recent Vision-Language-Action models under a unified protocol, establishing baselines for capability-specific performance, robustness, and data efficiency. items.title: Concurrent two-scale topology optimization of printable bone scaffolds via rectified-flow generation and exact latent-space refinement
items.summary: arXiv:2610.25565v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Bone scaffolds must reconcile a macroscale mechanical response with microscale geometric feasibility, yet conventional approaches to their design restrict attainable constitutive properties. In human femoral reconstruction, multiscale concurrent optimization produces a cortical mid-shaft scaffold with porosity 63\% while satisfying the compliance constraint within 2\% under walking and stair-climbing loads. It achieves an 84\% porosity on a proximal cancellous scaffold with strain-energy deviations below 0.25\% under the same loads. Analysis of the learned representations reveals distinct architectural families in latent space. Further, the attention heads of the rectified-flow transformer specialize for spatial shifts -- learning the analogue of a finite-difference stencil -- and coordinate symmetries, with ablations showing their influence on generated topologies. items.title: CheXFuse: Guided Differential Joint Attention Fusion for Robust Multimodal Chest X-Ray Classification in Data-Scarce Medical Settings
items.summary: arXiv:2610.25617v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: A central challenge in multimodal learning is how to fuse modalities that differ substantially in predictive strength. When one modality provides a much stronger representation than another, indiscriminate cross-modal interaction can introduce weak, redundant, or unstable signals, limiting or even degrading performance relative to the strongest unimodal representation. To address this problem, we propose CheXFuse, a multimodal fusion framework based on Guided Differential Joint Attention (GuDJA). CheXFuse combines image and text token representations within a joint multimodal sequence, where learned token guidance emphasizes informative representations and differential attention reduces less useful attention responses. We evaluate CheXFuse on the Indiana University (IU) Chest X-ray dataset, using binary (normal vs. abnormal) classification as the downstream task. Experiments are conducted under both original-report and masked-report settings, with the latter serving as a controlled stress test under reduced textual informativeness. CheXFuse with GuDJA achieves the strongest mean overall performance across the evaluated baselines and ablations, reaching 95.73% accuracy, 95.79% F1-score, 96.54% recall, and 95.28% sensitivity at 95% specificity (Sens@95Spec) with original reports, and 95.58%, 95.60%, 95.60%, and 94.34%, respectively, under masked reports. These results suggest that GuDJA provides a promising fusion strategy under asymmetric or partially reduced modality informativeness.

items.title: Clean Forcing: Drift-Resistant Autoregressive Video Diffusion with a Frozen Base
items.summary: arXiv:2610.25634v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Autoregressive (AR) video diffusion models generate streaming video of arbitrary length by conditioning each new chunk of frames on those already generated. However, they suffer from exposure bias, where a model trained on clean context must continue from its own imperfect outputs, and errors compound until quality collapses within seconds (drift). Existing methods either require cluster-scale base retraining, apply training-free inference corrections with inconsistent results, or train frozen-base correctors for sampling and cache errors. We instead find that drift is largely deterministic and therefore learnable, as holding the noisy state fixed while varying only the history reveals a counterfactual velocity gap that is ~95% systematic across noise seeds. Based on this observation, we introduce Clean Forcing, which trains a 5.9M-parameter LoRA corrector on the frozen base model to regress this gap, with a closed-loop stage that adds DAgger-style aggregation and a drift-contraction objective to expose the corrector to its own rollouts. Because the clean histories can be the base model's own single-shot generations, training needs no real videos, and the merged corrector adds no inference cost. In 50 s text-to-video generation, Clean Forcing reduces {\Delta}-drift from +11.3 to +1.65 without real video and to -0.16 with 40 real clips, improving on the best published result of +3.57 with over 150x less data. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Clean Forcing outperforms prior methods in aesthetic quality and data efficiency with reduced drift for long-horizon video generation.

items.title: Uncertainty-Gated SHAP-Dirichlet Refinement for MRI-Based Depression Classification
items.summary: arXiv:2610.25635v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Structural MRI-based classification of major depressive disorder (MDD) remains challenging due to subtle, heterogeneous anatomical changes. Gains were concentrated among low-confidence cases, with significant improvements in calibration. The method also benefited an RBF support vector machine but not logistic regression or random forests. Ablations confirmed the importance of uncertainty gating and soft fusion. Dirichlet evidence identified baseline errors (AUROC 0.62), while deferring 50% of cases increased retained-case accuracy to approximately 75%. These findings support selective explanation-guided refinement as a practical approach to improving prediction reliability and facilitating expert triage in MDD classification.
